Financial Inclusion and Credit Impacts on Crop Production in Ghana

Mark Appiah-Twumasi; Francis Tsiboe; Aisha Adam; Sylvanus Gaku; Peter Quartey

Abstract

Financial-inclusion policy in sub-Saharan Africa rests on the premise that credit moves smallholders toward best-practice technology. We ask whether it does in Ghana, using the 2012/13 and 2016/17 Ghana Living Standards Survey: 15,860 crop farmers, 8.9% in borrowing households, with group-specific stochastic frontiers enveloped by a metafrontier and credit users matched one-to-one to non-users. Contrary to that premise, credit users’ technology set lies 5.3 percentage points farther from the best-practice frontier than matched non-users’; technical efficiency within groups differs little and inconsistently in sign; and meta-frontier efficiency is 2.9 points lower, almost entirely from that gap. They also apply fewer purchased inputs per hectare without producing less. The gap is robust to specification and pervasive across subgroups, cocoa excepted. These are associations, not causal effects. Most loans are informal and fewer than one in three financed farming: the question is less how much credit reaches farms than what it buys.

Keywords: financial inclusion; credit; mobile money; technical efficiency; meta-stochastic frontier; Ghana

JEL Classification: G21, G51, O13, Q12, Q14

1. Introduction

Financial inclusion, understood as access to and use of savings, credit, payment and insurance services, is a standard instrument of development policy, and the case for it is pressed hardest in economies whose output and employment rest on smallholder agriculture. Account ownership among adults in developing economies has widened substantially over the past decade, but unevenly, and rural and farming households remain among the least served [1], [2]. In sub-Saharan Africa the shortfall is largest, inclusion tracks income, schooling, age and gender most sharply [3], and the recent widening has come through mobile money rather than through banks [4], [5]. It is also where meta-analytic evidence on African agriculture finds farms operating persistently below best practice, with access to inputs and improved technology among the recurring explanations [6]. Ghana sits squarely in this pattern: the two rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS) used here record the same widening among rural households and a shift in the institutions through which they save and borrow [7], [8].

The economic case for extending these services to farmers rests on the liquidity constraint. Smallholders face lumpy, seasonally concentrated outlays on planting material, fertilizer, agro-chemicals and hired labour months before harvest income arrives, and households that cannot borrow against the harvest under-apply inputs, mis-time them or forgo technologies whose fixed costs they cannot pre-finance [9], [10], [11]. Credit that relaxes this constraint should, in principle, let farms adopt the practices of the best-performing producers and operate nearer to the best-practice production frontier, with the gains for productivity and food security that a large efficiency literature on African agriculture anticipates [6], [12].

Whether it does so in practice depends on which margin of farm performance one examines, and the two margins call for different policy responses. Output differences among farmers arise from two distinct sources: some farmers operate a less productive technology set than the best-performing group, and some use whatever technology they have less efficiently. The meta-stochastic frontier (MSF) framework separates these margins by benchmarking group-specific frontiers against a common metafrontier, so that the technology gap ratio (TGR) captures the productive capacity of a group’s technology relative to best practice, technical efficiency (TE) captures how well its members exploit it, and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE), measures overall performance against best practice. If credit users differ from non-users mainly in the technology they operate, the relevant instruments concern input systems, mechanization services and the terms on which a loan can be turned into farm investment; if they differ mainly in efficiency, the constraints lie in management, information and the timing of input use. A single production frontier estimated over both groups cannot tell these apart, because it forces both onto one technology and attributes every difference to inefficiency. Applications of the framework to Ghanaian crop production show that the two margins are empirically separable and that their relative weight varies across ecologies, crops, operator gender and age [13], [14], [15], [16]; the same decomposition has been applied to variety adoption in Ghana [17] and to credit access among cocoa farmers in Nigeria [18], but not, to our knowledge, to credit use in a nationally representative sample of Ghanaian farms.

The Ghanaian evidence on credit and farm performance is instead largely crop-specific, regional and cross-sectional, and it points in different directions. The one experimental exception is also the closest counterpart to the question asked here: randomizing capital grants and rainfall-index insurance among maize farmers in northern Ghana, [19] find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of risk rather than of liquidity, a design that establishes which constraint binds — something the observational comparison drawn here cannot do — for one crop in one region and for credit that is offered rather than sought. Elsewhere the record is observational. Participation in input-credit schemes in northern Ghana raised fertilizer and labour use among maize farmers with only modest output gains and no detectable income effect [20]; bank-linked credit did not raise the technical efficiency of smallholder rice producers relative to non-borrowers [21]; formal and informal financing arrangements were associated with higher technical or economic efficiency among maize producers [22], [23], [24]; and a broader indicator of financial inclusion has been linked to smallholder productivity [25]. Two features of that observational literature limit what can be concluded from it. First, each study estimates a single frontier for borrowers and non-borrowers, so an efficiency difference may be a technology difference in disguise. Second, borrowers are not a random draw of farmers, and comparisons that do not first balance who borrows against who does not conflate the correlates of borrowing with any association of borrowing itself. Two further features of rural credit complicate the interpretation of any credit contrast. Loans are fungible, so a loan recorded against a farm household need not reach the farm [26], and the population that uses credit differs from the population that has access to it, since demand-side constraints can bind as tightly as supply-side ones [27].

Ghana between 2012/13 and 2016/17 is a useful setting in which to ask the question in these terms, because inclusion widened on some margins and not on others. Among the crop farmers studied here, formal account ownership rose from 25.3% to 36.2% between the two rounds, yet the share of operators who applied for a loan stayed below one in ten (9.6% and 9.8%), the modal reason for not applying was that no loan was needed, lending shifted toward group-based schemes, and in 2012/13 only 29.0% of the loans held by farm households were reported as taken for agricultural purposes (Section 3). The households that borrow are therefore a small group whose loans are, for the most part, not farm loans, and any account of what credit does for crop production has to be consistent with that record.

This paper asks three questions. First, do farm households that use credit operate a different crop production technology from comparable households that do not, as reflected in input elasticities and returns to scale? Second, where their performance differs, does the difference arise from the technology set they operate (TGR), from the efficiency with which they operate it (TE), or from both? Third, do these associations depend on which household member holds the loan, on the other financial services the household uses, and on operator gender, age and education, crop and region?

To answer them we pool the farmer-level records of GLSS waves 6 (2012/13) and 7 (2016/17), the two rounds that administer the credit and financial-services module in comparable form, and reconstruct credit use from the original questionnaires. The sample, drawn from a nationally representative survey, comprises 15,860 crop farm operators, of whom 8.9% live in a household in which the operator, a spouse, a child or another member applied for a loan in the preceding twelve months, was granted it and recorded a positive amount; this household-level indicator is the preferred treatment because liquidity is pooled within the farm household. We estimate separate translog stochastic frontiers for credit-using and non-using households, envelop them with a stochastic metafrontier, and form the comparison on a sample in which each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user matched exactly on survey wave, region, agro-ecological zone, locality type and operator gender and closely on demographic, household, cropping and financial-inclusion characteristics [28], [29], [30], following a small literature that combines the metafrontier with matching where the technology group is self-selected [31], [32], [33]. Standard errors for every quantity, including each group difference, come from a cluster jackknife over enumeration areas that re-runs matching and estimation in every replicate. Because the GLSS records credit use rather than credit access, offers no credible instrument for household borrowing, and cannot balance unobserved determinants of borrowing such as managerial ability, risk preference or standing with lenders, we interpret every difference reported here as an association conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as a causal effect of credit; Section 4 sets out what that interpretation permits.

The results do not conform to the liquidity-constraint story that motivates the expansion of rural credit. Credit users’ group frontier does differ from non-users’, with a markedly larger family-labour elasticity and higher returns to scale, but relative to the common best-practice frontier, credit-using households operate a less productive technology set, not a more productive one. In the matched sample their technology gap ratio averages 0.877 against 0.929 for matched non-users, a shortfall of 5.3 percentage points that keeps its sign under every definition of who in the household holds the loan, under alternative matching distances, functional forms, efficiency estimators and aggregation rules, among account holders and non-holders alike, and in nearly every gender, age, education, crop and regional subgroup, cocoa producers being the one clear exception. The technical-efficiency difference within groups is small by comparison and its sign is not stable across specifications, so the lower meta-frontier efficiency of credit users, a shortfall of between 2.9 and 4.3 percentage points depending on the specification, is a technology gap rather than a management gap. Balancing the two groups on observables removes most of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers but little of the technology gap, and matched credit users apply less fertilizer, planting material, hired labour and pesticide per hectare than their comparators without a significantly different value of output per hectare. Section 5 weighs the readings the data can speak to: that borrowing households are not, as a group, the ones operating the best-practice technology; that most household credit finances activity off the farm; that selection into borrowing on characteristics the survey does not record cannot be excluded; and that the comparison is between users and non-users rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first nationally representative evidence for Ghana that decomposes the performance difference between credit-using and non-using farm households into a technology margin and an efficiency margin, so that a lower technology gap ratio and an unchanged technical efficiency can be told apart; the existing evidence, confined to single crops, regions and frontiers, cannot make that distinction. Second, it measures credit at the household level, reports how the contrast changes when the borrower is the operator, the spouse or another member, and combines the metafrontier with matching and a full-pipeline jackknife, so that the borrower/non-borrower contrast is drawn between observably comparable households and carries the uncertainty of the pairing as well as of the estimation. Third, it reconstructs the financial-services modules of the GLSS to document the state of financial inclusion among crop farmers and uses that detail to examine whether the credit association differs among households that are otherwise financially included, and across operator, crop and regional subgroups, which is the information a policy that bundles credit with payment, advisory or risk services would need [12], [34]. The finding that borrowing households operate a technology farther inside the national frontier than comparable non-borrowers reframes the policy question from how much credit reaches farm households to what the credit they already obtain is buying.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data, the construction of the credit and financial-service indicators from the GLSS questionnaires, and the descriptive statistics of credit users and non-users. Section 3 documents the state of financial inclusion and credit access among Ghanaian crop farmers over the two rounds and draws out what it implies for the design. Section 4 states the hypotheses, presents the meta-stochastic frontier specification and the matching design, delimits what the design identifies, and describes inference and the robustness programme. Section 5 reports diagnostics, output elasticities, the technology and efficiency decomposition, its interpretation, robustness checks and heterogeneity, with discussion integrated. Section 6 concludes with the implications for policy and research.

2. Data sources and sample description

2.1 Data sources and sample construction

We use farm-level microdata from the sixth and seventh rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS), fielded in 2012/13 (GLSS6) and 2016/17 (GLSS7) [7], [8]. Both rounds are repeated cross-sections drawn through a two-stage design in which enumeration areas are selected first and households within them second, and they are the only two rounds that administer the household financial-services module in comparable form, which fixes the study window. Farm, household and operator variables come from the consolidated farmer-level GLSS dataset of [35], which harmonizes the agricultural modules across rounds and has supported a series of analyses of crop production technology and efficiency in Ghana [13], e.g., [14], [15], [16], [36]. The unit of observation is the farm operator, the household member who manages the household’s plots. Following the consolidated dataset, we retain crop producers whose yields (kg/ha) fall between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within each survey round and crop, so that extreme values do not drive the frontier estimates. Each operator contributes one pooled record covering all crops grown, which is the record the frontier analysis uses, and the crop-specific records that underlie the crop rows of Table 1.

Two further restrictions apply upstream of the analysis, and both are complete-case restrictions. First, the harmonized financial module retains operators aged at least eighteen with recorded age, schooling, account-ownership and insurance status, because these items enter the financial-inclusion index and the matching covariates described in Section 2.3, and the index itself is estimated on complete cases of its indicator set. Second, the matching stage of Section 4.3 requires complete information on every matching covariate. The pooled analysis sample, after the first of these restrictions, comprises 15,860 farm operators, of whom 1,405 live in households that used credit as defined in Section 2.2 and 14,455 do not (Table 1). Operators cultivate at least one of banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton/kenaf, maize, millet, oil palm, groundnut, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other minor crops, and the sample spans the ten administrative regions of the period and all agro-ecological zones. Crop output value and planting-material expenditure are expressed per hectare in real terms, as labelled in Table 1. No survey weights are applied, either to the descriptive statistics in Tables 1 to 3 and S1 to S2 or to the estimation; the statistics therefore describe the surveyed crop producers rather than population totals, although the GLSS is designed to be representative at the national and regional levels.

2.2 Measuring credit use and the other financial-service indicators

The consolidated dataset does not carry the financial-services module, so the credit and financial-service indicators are rebuilt from the original GLSS questionnaires. Using the enumeration-area, household and member identifiers preserved in both files, we extract the items of Part B, Section 12a (credit, banking, use of financial services and insurance) for every member of a farm household and merge them to the farmer-level file. Table S0 in the appendix documents, for each round, the source item, the question wording, the response options and the mapping to each analysis variable. These items serve three purposes in the paper: they define the credit indicator described next, they describe the financial-services environment of crop farmers in Section 3 (Tables 2 and 3), and they supply the dimensions along which Section 5 examines heterogeneity in the credit contrasts (Table 6 and Figure 2).

Credit use is defined for an individual as the conjunction of three conditions in the twelve months preceding the interview: the person applied for a loan (s12aq7 in both rounds); the application was granted (s12aq8 in GLSS6, s12aq8a to s12aq8c in GLSS7); and a positive loan amount was recorded (s12aq10 in both rounds). Because the questionnaire elicits loan detail only from applicants whose loan was granted, requiring only a granted application, or only a positive amount, reproduces the indicator observation for observation; the conjunction matters for what it excludes rather than for what it includes. A person who applied and was refused, or whose application was still pending, is a non-user. Relaxing the criterion to any application regardless of outcome would raise the operator-level rate from 6.1% to 9.7%, but that is a different construct, one that pools refused and pending applicants with those who received funds.

Our preferred treatment is defined at the household level: a farm operator is a credit user if the operator, the operator’s spouse, a child of the operator, or any other household member satisfies the individual criterion. Aggregating to the household reflects the pooling of liquidity within farm households. A loan taken by a spouse relaxes the same cash constraint on the same farm, and the technology the frontier analysis characterizes is the household’s, not the operator’s borrowing record. By this definition 8.9% of operators live in a household that used credit. The operator personally satisfied the criterion in 6.1% of the sample, so that in about 31% of credit-using households the loan was held by a spouse, a child or another member rather than by the operator; the household categories overlap, since a household may contain more than one borrower, and Table S1 reports the number of operators in each. The farmer-only variant, which counts only the operator’s own borrowing, is a strict subset of the household measure, because no operator borrows in a household recorded as having no credit, and it reclassifies 2.7% of the sample from user to non-user. Unless stated otherwise, “credit user” refers to the household measure. Section 5 reports the frontier comparison under the household definition and under the operator-only, spouse and other-member definitions (Table 5), and Tables S1 and S2 describe the characteristics and trends of the corresponding subsamples.

Three features of what the indicator measures bear on how the results should be read. First, it records the use of credit, not access to it. The credit-constraints literature classifies households by direct elicitation of whether they were rationed, discouraged or unconstrained at prevailing terms [9], [10]; the GLSS module records refusals and, for non-applicants, the main reason for not applying (Table 3), but a household that could have borrowed and chose not to is pooled with one that could not borrow at all. The contrast we estimate is therefore between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained, a distinction Section 4.4 makes precise. Second, the indicator counts a loan from any source and for any purpose. Although the screening question refers to a loan from a financial institution, the source codes that follow include friends and relatives and group-based schemes, and Section 3 shows that these supply most of the loans farm households hold and that only a minority of loans are reported as taken for farming. The indicator should accordingly be read as household credit use rather than as agricultural credit, the construct that most of the Ghanaian studies reviewed in Section 1 examine [20], [21], [22], [24], and household credit is fungible, so a loan reported for one purpose may finance another [26]. Third, the twelve-month recall window is not tied to the cropping calendar, so a loan may have been taken after the season’s input decisions were made. The reliance of the classification on self-reported borrowing, and the likely direction of any reporting error, are discussed in Section 4.3.

Two asymmetries between the rounds bound the indicator further. The rounds do not code loan outcomes identically: GLSS6 records a binary granted or not granted, whereas GLSS7 adds a third status, “processing”, which the indicator treats as non-use because no loan had been disbursed. This status applies to 2.4% of GLSS7 applicants and has no GLSS6 counterpart, so cross-round comparisons of application outcomes in Section 3 set a two-way classification against a three-way one. In addition, GLSS7 elicits the status, source, purpose and collateral of up to three loans but records a single loan amount, so where an applicant reports several loans the amount cannot be attributed to a particular one; GLSS6, with one loan slot, has no such ambiguity. Neither asymmetry affects the treatment indicator, which depends only on whether some loan was granted and disbursed.

Credit is one dimension of financial inclusion, and the same module supplies the others. From Section 12a we also construct indicators of formal account ownership, the type of institution and account held, transaction products used and insurance cover, and, from the GLSS community questionnaire, the distance from the farmer’s community to the nearest bank, motorable road and public transport (Table S0). Section 3 uses these to describe the financial-services environment of crop farmers, and Section 5 uses account ownership and the other service indicators as dimensions along which the credit contrasts are disaggregated.

2.3 Production variables, matching covariates and the financial-inclusion index

The frontier analysis of Section 4 uses the real value of crop output as the dependent variable and six inputs: cultivated land, planting material, family labour, hired labour, fertilizer and pesticide. Table 1 reports these in the units in which they are summarized, namely real GH₵ per hectare for output and planting material, adult equivalents for family labour, man-days per hectare for hired labour, kilograms per hectare for fertilizer and litres per hectare for pesticide, together with indicators for the use of mechanized equipment and irrigation. The determinants of inefficiency (Table S4) are the operator’s gender, age and years of schooling, land ownership, the crop diversification index, mechanization, receipt of extension advice, and fixed effects for ecological zone and survey round; credit is not among them, because it defines the groups whose frontiers are compared. The matching of Section 4.3 draws on a wider set of characteristics: the operator’s age, schooling, marital status, religion, ethnicity and relationship to the household head; household size in adult equivalents, the female share of adult equivalents and the dependency ratio; crop diversification and the share of cultivated area under each major crop; land ownership; and a financial-inclusion index, with exact matching on survey round, region, ecological zone, rural or urban locality and operator gender. Table S5 in the appendix defines every variable entering the frontier, the inefficiency term and the matching distance, states the unit in which it is measured, and gives the sign expected of it where theory or the Ghanaian evidence implies one.

The financial-inclusion index summarizes the non-credit dimensions of financial connectedness, and Note S1 in the appendix documents its construction in full. It is the first principal component of fourteen indicators: the operator’s years of schooling, whether the operator works in the financial sector, whether another household member does, ownership of an account with a financial institution or contribution to a savings scheme, and ten indicators of insurance cover, spanning vehicle, health, funeral, property, business, travel, life, pension, education and other endowment or investment policies (Table S0). The component is not fitted once on the pooled sample. It is fitted separately within each survey-round and locality stratum, that is within the rural and the urban part of each of GLSS6 and GLSS7, and because the sign and the scale of a principal component are arbitrary, each stratum’s score is placed on the metric of the component fitted to the pooled sample by regressing the pooled score on the stratum score and retaining the fitted values, which fixes orientation as well as scale before the stratum scores are combined. That rescaled component is then min-max scaled over the pooled sample onto the unit interval, and it is the scaled index, not the raw component, that enters the matching distance of Section 4.3. Table S6 reports the first-component loadings and the share of variance the component explains in each stratum, which is also where the limits of the construct are visible: the component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in its indicator set, and the set itself is not identical across rounds, since travel insurance has too little variation to enter in either 2016/17 stratum and the account item recognizes mobile money only in that round. The index is a covariate used to balance credit users and non-users on their broader engagement with financial services; it is not the treatment, and no result in this paper is reported by index category. Heterogeneity in the credit association across financial services is instead examined directly on the observed indicators, formal account ownership above all (Figure 2 and Table 6).

2.4 Descriptive statistics

Table 1 summarizes the farmer, production and household characteristics of the pooled sample and of credit users and non-users, together with the annual percentage change in each characteristic between the two rounds; daggers mark characteristics on which users and non-users differ at the 5% level. The average operator is 47 years old with 4.3 years of schooling, and 25% of operators are women. Households average 5.5 adult equivalents with a dependency ratio of 1.43. Farms are small, at 1.84 ha on average, consistent with the smallholder profile reported in national statistics [37]; 63% of operators own the land they farm, and the crop diversification index averages 0.47. Mean crop output value is GH₵ 1,299 per hectare across all crops, with wide dispersion across crops. Purchased-input use is low and uneven: operators spend about GH₵ 139 per hectare on planting material, hire about 19 man-days per hectare, and apply about 267 kg of fertilizer and 20 litres of pesticide per hectare, the fertilizer and pesticide means being dominated by a small number of very large values, as their standard deviations show; only 5% use mechanized equipment and 2% irrigate. This is a production environment in which output depends chiefly on land and household labour, and in which the lumpy, liquidity-intensive investments that credit is expected to finance are the exception rather than the rule.

Credit users differ from non-users on a small number of characteristics, and they are the characteristics that matter most for who borrows and how farms perform. Users are younger (45.8 against 47.4 years) and markedly more educated (6.1 against 4.1 years), they are less likely to own the land they farm (59% against 63%), and they hire more labour per hectare (25 against 19 man-days). Output value per hectare across all crops does not differ significantly between the groups (GH₵ 1,419 against GH₵ 1,287), and neither do farm size, household size, the dependency ratio, crop diversification, the share of women among operators, planting-material expenditure, family labour, fertilizer or pesticide intensity, mechanization or irrigation. Where crop-specific output values differ, the sign is not uniform: non-users record higher values per hectare for rice, groundnut and yam, and users for cocoyam. On the observable production record, then, borrowers are not a systematically more productive or more input-intensive group; they are a younger, more schooled group that is less likely to own its land and relies more on hired labour.

The trend columns show that the two groups also changed differently between the rounds, and, because the survey is a repeated cross-section, these trends describe changes in the composition and practices of the two groups rather than changes within households. In the pooled sample, real output value per hectare rose by about 11% per year, and schooling, landholding, land ownership, planting-material expenditure and both family and hired labour use increased, while crop diversification and mechanization declined; the pooled trends in fertilizer and pesticide intensity are imprecisely estimated. Schooling rose among non-users, by 5.5% per year, but was flat among users, so the education gap between the groups narrowed; household size fell among non-users and rose among users; and land ownership rose faster among users (9.3% against 3.6% per year). Fertilizer intensity rose by 16.3% per year among credit users, a trend that is precisely estimated, whereas the corresponding trend among non-users is not, although the two trends are not statistically distinguishable from each other. The composition of the credit-using group is therefore not fixed across rounds, which is one reason the matching in Section 4.3 is performed exactly within survey round.

The profile of borrowing households also depends on who in the household borrows (Table S1). Where the operator is the borrower, operators are younger (45.5 years) and more educated (6.5 years) than the pooled average, less likely to own their land (57%) and hire more labour per hectare. Where the spouse is the borrower, households are larger (6.8 adult equivalents against 5.5 in the pooled sample), more diversified and more likely to irrigate, and only 12% of operators are women, so spousal credit is in most such households a wife’s loan on a husband-operated farm. Households in which a child holds the credit are too few to support separate inference. These contrasts are one reason the household definition is preferred and the person-specific definitions are reported alongside it: restricting attention to the operator’s own borrowing would drop the spouse- and other-member-borrower households, which differ from operator-borrower households in size and cropping pattern.

Taken together, the descriptive evidence carries two implications for the empirical strategy. First, credit users differ from non-users in age, schooling, tenure and hired labour, characteristics that also predict technology choice and technical efficiency, and their composition shifts between rounds, so an unconditional comparison of frontier outcomes would confound the association with credit with differences in who borrows; the pool of non-users is large, with about 10 non-users per user, so a close counterpart for each borrower is available, and Section 4.3 pairs them before estimation. Second, whether borrowing and non-borrowing households operate the same production technology cannot be settled from sample means, and the financing environment described in Section 3 gives reason to doubt it; Section 4.2 therefore estimates separate group frontiers and benchmarks both against a common metafrontier, so that differences in technology can be separated from differences in technical efficiency. Whether credit-using households in fact operate closer to or farther from the best-practice frontier is the empirical question the remainder of the paper addresses.

3. The state of financial inclusion and credit access

Sections 4 and 5 compare the production technology and technical efficiency of farm households that used credit with those of comparable households that did not. How that comparison should be read depends on what borrowing means in this setting: who has access to financial services and through which institutions, who lends to farm households, on what terms and for what stated purposes, and why most farmers do not borrow at all. This section establishes that context from the same crop farmers used in the estimation. Table 2 reports, for 2012/13 and 2016/17, account ownership and the reasons non-holders give for having no account, the institutions and products through which accounts are held, the distance from the farmer’s community to financial and transport infrastructure, and insurance cover; Table 3 follows the loan cycle from application through outcome, source, purpose and collateral to the reasons given for refusal and for not applying. Each entry is an unweighted share of the farm operators in a round or, where the item applies only to a subgroup, of that subgroup (account holders, non-holders, borrowers, rejected applicants, non-applicants); the items and response options are documented in Table S0. Three patterns organize what follows. Access to basic financial services widened appreciably between the rounds, and the widening came through mobile money and savings channels rather than through banks. The use of credit did not widen, and the borrowing that occurred was mostly informal or group-based and, where its purpose can be observed, mostly directed to non-farm ends. And the constraint that non-borrowers report is more often the absence of a perceived need than an institutional barrier.

The first of these patterns is visible in the account-ownership rows of Table 2, and it is a widening from a low base. The share of crop farmers holding an account with a financial institution or contributing to a savings scheme rose from 25.3% in 2012/13 to 36.2% in 2016/17, a gain of 10.9 percentage points (Table 2), consistent with the expansion documented in the national survey reports for the same rounds [7], [8] and with the growth of account ownership across sub-Saharan Africa over the period [1], [2], [5]. Even so, 64% of farmers had no account of any kind at the end of the period, so ownership remained a minority status in this population throughout. Part of the increase reflects the instrument as well as behaviour: the 2016/17 questionnaire recognizes mobile money as an account-holding institution, an item the 2012/13 questionnaire did not carry (Table S0), and mobile money turns out to account for a large share of the accounts held in the later round, as the composition of those accounts, taken up below, shows.

Who remained outside follows a pattern documented across African countries, in which income and schooling are the strongest correlates of being banked [3], and the reasons non-holders themselves give point the same way, to income rather than to institutions. Not having enough money or income was cited by 58.2% of non-holders in 2012/13 and 60.4% in 2016/17, and an irregular income by a further 21.9% and 19.4%, so that income-related reasons account for about 80% of non-holders in the later round, in line with the global pattern in which insufficient funds is the most commonly reported barrier to account ownership [1], [2]. Mistrust of financial institutions is the only other reason cited by more than one non-holder in ten, and it rose from 12.3% to 14.3%. Distance, by contrast, was cited by 4.9% of non-holders in 2012/13 and only 2.9% in 2016/17, and cumbersome procedures by little more than one non-holder in a hundred in either round. By farmers’ own account, further expansion of physical access would address a small and shrinking part of non-ownership; the binding constraint is the level and regularity of income, which is bound up with the same seasonality and risk of farm income that motivate borrowing in the first place.

If what keeps farmers out of the account market is income rather than institutions, the institutions on offer to those who are in it were nonetheless changing shape. The channels through which farmers hold accounts shifted markedly between the rounds, and the shift was driven by mobile money rather than by banks. Commercial, community and rural banks served 68.1% of account holders in 2012/13 and 49.5% in 2016/17. Because ownership rose over the same period, the share of all farmers with a bank account was almost unchanged, at about 17% and 18% respectively; the growth in inclusion came from elsewhere. Mobile money, not elicited in the 2012/13 instrument, was reported by 35.6% of account holders in 2016/17, second only to banks within four years of its appearance in the questionnaire and consistent with the rapid diffusion of phone-based finance documented across the region [4], [5]. Susu schemes remained a stable secondary channel, at 14.5% and 16.1% of account holders, while savings and loans companies (10.8% to 9.7%) and cooperatives or credit unions (5.5% to 3.6%) lost ground.

What those accounts are used for changed less than who provides them, and it is a narrow use: accounts store money rather than move it. Savings accounts were held by 59.9% of account holders in 2012/13 and 57.8% in 2016/17, current or cheque accounts by about 14%, and investment accounts by fewer than one holder in a hundred. That the mix is dominated by savings fits the place formal institutions occupy in Ghanaian household finance, as somewhere to hold resources rather than to transact, a margin on which household saving has been shown to respond to the inflows a household receives, remittances among them [38]. Among transaction products, cheque-book use rose from 11.7% to 21.9% of account holders, but ATM cards (3.2% in 2016/17) and electronic banking (0.3%) had barely registered. The financial inclusion that broadened among crop farmers over this period was therefore a widening of savings and payment access, increasingly through mobile money, rather than a deepening of credit or of transactional banking. Account ownership is accordingly a weak proxy for credit access, which is why the analysis treats credit use, rather than account ownership or the composite financial-inclusion index of Section 2.3 whose construction and loadings are documented in Note S1, as the grouping variable for the frontiers (Section 4), and returns to account ownership and the other service indicators only as dimensions along which the credit contrast may differ (Figure 2 and Table 6). Table 2 also reports how account holders first learned of their institution; that block is not drawn on in the text because the mapping of its response categories is under review, as the note to Table S0 records.

The physical infrastructure behind these accounts improved over the same period, which is the counterpart of the declining share of non-holders who cite distance. The average distance from a farmer’s community to the nearest bank fell by 5.9 km, from 17.5 km in 2012/13 to 11.5 km in 2016/17; the distance to a motorable road fell from 0.9 km to 0.6 km and to public transport from 4.7 km to 2.5 km (Table 2). These are community-level measures from the community questionnaire (Table S0), so they describe the environment a farmer faces rather than the farmer’s own travel, but the direction is clear: by the later round, whatever kept farm households out of the credit market, it was less and less the cost of reaching a lender.

Against that improvement in reach, the risk-pooling side of financial inclusion did not move at all. Insurance cover is thin and confined to health. Enrolment in health insurance rose from 12.4% to 18.1% of farmers and is the only product with any reach; life cover fell from 1.8% to 1.2% and pension plans from 1.1% to 0.3%, and every other product covered roughly one farmer in a hundred or fewer. The survey instrument records no crop or livestock insurance at all (Table S0), so the production risk that borrowing exposes a farm household to is, within the products observed here, uninsured. This is not for want of demand: Ghanaian and comparative evidence finds substantial willingness among farmers to take up index-based agricultural insurance when suitable products are offered [39], [40], [41]. Uninsured production risk is a recognized reason why farm households under-invest in yield-raising inputs even when liquidity is available [11], and it belongs alongside the liquidity-relaxation story when the credit contrasts are interpreted in Section 5: a household that borrows in this environment adds a fixed repayment obligation to an uninsured income stream.

None of this widening reached the credit market. Credit use did not move with access, and Table 3, which reports the farm operator’s own loan record, shows why the two margins have to be kept apart: 9.6% of operators applied for a loan in the twelve months before the 2012/13 interview and 9.8% before the 2016/17 interview. Conditional on applying, 64.3% of applications were granted in the earlier round and 61.9% in the later one, so that operators with an accepted loan made up 6.2% and 6.1% of all farmers. The share of all farmers whose application was refused fell from 0.9% to 0.5%, but because approval conditional on applying did not rise, the fall in recorded refusals does not indicate more generous lending; part of it reflects the “processing” status that only the 2016/17 instrument offers, which applied to 2.4% of that round’s applicants (Section 2.2). Extending the definition from the operator to any household member, as the treatment of Section 2 does, raises the credit-use rate to 8.9% of the pooled sample, still a small minority. The flat application rate against a rising ownership rate is the first fact to carry forward: whatever the account expansion of this period did, it did not draw more farm households into borrowing.

The borrowing that does occur, moreover, has little to do with the institutions whose reach expanded. Where farmers borrow, they borrow mainly outside the formal banking sector, and increasingly through groups. Group-based microfinance or lending rose from 23.8% to 39.2% of loans between the rounds and became the single largest source. Friends and relatives supplied 33.9% of loans in 2012/13 and 28.5% in 2016/17, informal credit and savings groups a stable 14.3% and 14.9%, and formal lenders, that is banks and other financial institutions, a declining 23.1% and 16.9%. Relational and group-based sources together supplied about 83% of loans in the later round. This is the pattern that the literature on smallholder finance in the region describes: formal agricultural lending remains a small part of rural credit [12], farmers assemble working capital through informal and semi-formal arrangements [23], and savings groups have become an important channel for small loans to poor households [42]. Its terms match its provenance. No guarantee was required for 67.7% of loans in 2012/13 and 77.1% in 2016/17, cash was the most common security where one was required (14.8% and 12.2%), and land secured only 3.0% and 0.8% of loans, so the asset most often discussed as smallholder collateral secured almost none in practice. Among the few applications that were refused, inability to provide collateral or a trusted guarantor remained the leading reason (42.9% and 46.4% of refusals), although these shares rest on few observations. Two consequences follow for identification. A loan intermediated through a group or a personal network is allocated on information the survey does not record, such as standing in the community and repayment history, and its presence in one household is unlikely to be independent of the terms available to its neighbours; Section 4.4 takes up both.

If the source of a loan says who allocated it, its stated purpose says where it went, and that bears directly on the interpretation of the credit indicator; the evidence is available on a comparable basis for 2012/13 only. In that round, when the purpose of a single loan was elicited and the tabulated categories are exhaustive, farming was the single most common stated purpose but accounted for under a third of loans (29.0%), followed by business (22.5%), education or training (16.7%) and ceremonies (13.0%), with debt repayment and other uses making up the remainder. The 2016/17 instrument elicits the purpose of up to three loans separately (Table S0), and the harmonized purpose categories printed in Table 3 for that round together cover only about 10% of accepted loans, so the apparent fall in every purpose share between rounds cannot be read as a change in behaviour, and we do not compare purposes across rounds. The 2012/13 distribution suffices for the point that matters here: most household borrowing in this population finances consumption, schooling, social obligations or non-farm enterprise rather than farm inputs, and even loans taken for farming are fungible with these other uses [26]. The credit indicator used in Sections 4 and 5 therefore identifies households that obtained liquidity, not households that invested in the farm, and the survey does not link a loan to the spending it financed.

That leaves the great majority of farmers, who did not borrow at all, and most of them do not describe themselves as rationed. Among farmers who did not apply for a loan, the share giving no need for one as the main reason rose from 55.4% in 2012/13 to 63.7% in 2016/17, while the share citing an institutional constraint, such as interest rates, collateral demands or the unavailability of the amount needed, fell from 37.2% to 28.6%; a financial constraint on the borrower’s side was cited by 1.8% and 5.2%. The stated institutional barrier thus receded over a period in which the application rate did not move. A stated absence of need should not be equated with an absence of constraint: survey-based classifications of credit rationing recognize that households that expect to be refused, that face high transaction costs, or that are unwilling to bear the repayment risk of an uninsured season report no demand and never apply, so that “no need” pools the genuinely unconstrained with the discouraged and the risk-rationed [9], [10], and the GLSS does not ask the follow-up questions that would separate them. What the pattern does establish is that the non-user group in the analysis is composed largely of households that, on their own account, chose not to borrow rather than households that were turned away, and that the bottleneck in this market sits at least as much on the demand side as on the supply side, which is the reading of agricultural finance that argues for aligning products with farmers’ production calendar and perceived needs rather than for expanding supply alone [12], [27].

Read as one record, running from account ownership through insurance to the loan cycle, four features of this setting shape the analysis that follows and fix where each is taken up. First, credit users are a small minority, and they differ from non-users in the financing environment they inhabit, with borrowing concentrated in group and relational channels whose availability varies across communities; comparing the two groups against a single frontier would attribute to managerial efficiency what may be a difference in the technology each group operates, which is the case for group frontiers and a common metafrontier (Section 4.2), for making the comparison within a sample constructed to be comparable (Section 4.3), and for the test of whether the two groups share a technology at all, reported among the diagnostics in Section 5.1. Second, the indicator distinguishes households that used credit from households that did not, and the modal non-user reports no need for a loan; the contrast estimated in Section 5 is therefore between borrowers and non-borrowers, not between the credit-constrained and the unconstrained, a limit that Section 4.4 makes explicit and that the loan-application row of Table 6 probes by narrowing the comparison to households in which the operator applied. Third, the loans observed are mostly unsecured, mostly informal or group-based and, where their purpose is recorded, mostly for non-farm uses; whether borrowing of this kind is associated with operating a technology nearer to best practice, with a different responsiveness of output to inputs, or with neither, is an empirical question rather than a presumption, and it is settled on the group-frontier elasticities and returns to scale of Table 4 in Section 5.2 and on the technology-gap and efficiency decomposition of Table 4 in Section 5.3, with the readings the data can and cannot support weighed in Section 5.4. Fourth, account ownership and mobile money spread while credit use and insurance did not, so borrowing households differ in the financial services that surround the loan; Section 5.6 asks whether the credit contrast differs between account holders and others and across the financial-service categories of Table 2 (Figure 2 and Table 6). The frontier estimates themselves are deferred to Section 5; what this section supplies is the record with which those estimates, and any reading of them, have to be consistent.

4. Empirical methods

Sections 2 and 3 established what the credit indicator measures and the environment in which it is measured. Credit use is uncommon, involving 8.9% of farm households; users are younger and better educated than non-users (Table 1); lending is increasingly intermediated through groups; most loans are not reported as farm loans; and the modal non-applicant reports no need for a loan (Table 3). A method that simply compared output per hectare between borrowers and non-borrowers would fold together three distinct things: differences in the production technology the two groups operate, differences in how well each group uses its own technology, and differences in who borrows. This section sets out how the analysis separates them. Section 4.1 states the mechanisms and the hypotheses they imply. Section 4.2 presents the meta-stochastic frontier that decomposes performance into technology and efficiency. Section 4.3 describes the matching that removes compositional differences on observables. Section 4.4 states what the resulting estimates do and do not identify, and Section 4.5 describes inference and the robustness programme.

4.1 Conceptual framework and hypotheses

Credit enters crop production through the liquidity constraint. A farm household that cannot borrow must finance seed, fertilizer, agro-chemicals and hired labour from its own savings or current income, at the point in the season when those resources are scarcest, and must bear the full downside risk of any investment it makes. That position is not incidental: the seasonality, spatial dispersion and covariate risk of rainfed cropping are the material conditions under which credit and insurance markets in tropical smallholder agriculture remain thin, interlinked or absent, so the terms on which a farm can finance a season are a structural feature of the production environment rather than a household-specific accident [43]. Credit can relax this constraint along two conceptually distinct margins. It can finance lumpy or indivisible investments, such as improved planting material, mechanized services or a switch of crop, that change the technology the farm operates; and it can finance the timely purchase of divisible inputs within a given technology, allowing the farm to operate nearer to the frontier of that technology [9], [10], [44]. The metafrontier framework of Section 4.2 is chosen because it maps onto this distinction: the technology gap ratio (TGR) measures the productive capacity of the technology a group operates relative to the best practice observed in the sample, and technical efficiency (TE) measures how close a farmer comes to the frontier of the group’s own technology. The Ghanaian evidence reviewed in Section 1 is mixed in part because it does not make this separation, since each of those studies estimates a single frontier for borrowers and non-borrowers and cannot distinguish a lower efficiency score from a different technology.

From the liquidity-constraint view we derive three hypotheses, stated so that the data can reject them. The first concerns the technology margin. If borrowing finances technology-embodying investment, the frontier of credit users should lie closer to the metafrontier than the frontier of non-users, so that credit use is associated with a higher TGR (H1). The second concerns the efficiency margin. Adoption financed by credit can outrun the agronomic knowledge, risk management and timely input delivery needed to use new inputs well, and repayment obligations can divert management attention or labour toward the activities that generate cash, so that borrowers, conditional on their own technology, produce farther below their frontier; evidence from Ghanaian cocoa shows how much the payoff to new practices depends on complementary training [45], and the case for bundling finance with agronomic and risk-management support rests on the same logic [12], [34]. We therefore hypothesize that credit use is associated with lower TE (H2), while noting that theory does not exclude the opposite sign, since credit can also permit inputs to be applied at the agronomically appropriate time and can loosen the risk-induced under-application that characterizes poor households facing uninsured consumption risk [11]. The third concerns the shape of the technology rather than the distance to it. Where credit finances working capital, it should raise the output response to the inputs whose timing is most sensitive to liquidity, land preparation and labour, more than to fertilizer, whose contribution is bounded by input quality and application practice that finance alone does not relax; we therefore expect credit users’ frontier to be more responsive to land and labour than to fertilizer, relative to non-users (H3). H1 and H2 are tested on the sign and significance of the credit-minus-no-credit differences in TGR and TE (Tables 4 and 5), and H3 on the differences in group-frontier elasticities (Table 4).

Two considerations visible in Section 3 temper the first hypothesis and make its sign an empirical question. Credit relaxes the farm’s liquidity constraint only if the loan, or the liquidity it frees, reaches the farm. Loans are fungible [26], only a minority of loans in these data are reported as taken for agricultural purposes (Table 3), and the treatment records borrowing rather than the ability to borrow, so a non-user who reports no need for a loan is not liquidity-constrained in the sense the theory requires. Who borrows is also not random, since lenders target and households self-select, increasingly through group-based schemes whose membership the survey does not record. If the borrowing households are not, as a group, those investing in farm technology, the TGR contrast can be null, and it can be negative if borrowing is concentrated among households whose farm technology is weaker for reasons the observables do not capture, such as distress borrowing after a shock or lender targeting of particular activities. A rejection of H1 is therefore informative about which of these conditions fails rather than a failure of the framework. Each mechanism also implies where the associations should be strongest, and the design measures those dimensions: complementary human capital should make credit more likely to reach the frontier, so the contrasts are reported by operator gender, age and education (Figure 3); crops differ in the cash-input intensity and lumpiness of their technologies, and regions in market access and in the density of financial infrastructure, so the contrasts are reported by major crop and region (Figure 4); and the interaction between credit and the other dimensions of financial inclusion, which Section 3 shows expanding faster than credit itself, is examined by contrasting households with and without a formal account (Figure 2) and within each of the financial-service categories described in Section 2.2 (Table 6). Because the design is observational (Section 4.4), every hypothesis is tested as an association rather than as an effect. The policy reading differs by outcome: if credit is associated with a narrower technology gap but lower efficiency, the case is for bundling credit with extension, risk instruments and reliable input delivery; if it is associated with a wider gap, the case is for asking what borrowing households are financing and whether the loans on offer are sized and timed for crop production [5], [27].

4.2 Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

Credit users and non-users may face different financing constraints and, plausibly, operate different production technologies. A single frontier fitted to both groups would fold technology differences into measured inefficiency. We therefore estimate a separate stochastic frontier for each group and benchmark both against a common metafrontier, following the two-step stochastic metafrontier of [46], which envelops the group-specific stochastic frontiers within a metafrontier that is itself stochastic rather than deterministic, so that the technology gap is an estimated quantity carrying its own error rather than a residual imposed by a deterministic envelope. What the framework delivers is the standard decomposition of producer performance in efficiency and productivity analysis [47]: it separates proximity to the best-practice technology, measured by the technology gap ratio (TGR), from efficiency within the group’s own technology, measured by technical efficiency (TE); their product is meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE). Credit status does not enter the frontier as a regressor. It defines the groups, \(j \in \{\text{credit user},\ \text{non-user}\}\), and thereby the frontier against which each farmer is assessed, so that the two frontiers are free to differ in every coefficient. This is the framework applied to GLSS data by earlier work on gender, age, crop and ecological differences in Ghanaian crop production [13], [14], [15], [16], here applied to credit.

For group \(j\) the stochastic frontier takes a translog form, which nests the Cobb-Douglas form and allows the input elasticities to vary with the input bundle:

\[ f^{j}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(y_{ijt}) = \beta_{0j} + \sum_{k} \beta_{kj}\ln(x_{kijt}) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skj}\ln(x_{kijt})\ln(x_{sijt}) + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} + v_{ijt} - u_{ijt} \]

\[ u_{ijt} \sim N^{+}\!\left(0,\ \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})\right),\qquad v_{ijt} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma_{vj}^{2}\right) \qquad\qquad (1) \]

Here \(y_{ijt}\) is the real value of crop output of the \(i\)th farm operator in group \(j\) in survey round \(t\); the inputs \(x_{kijt}\) are land, planting material, family labour, hired labour, fertilizer and pesticide; and \(h_{ijt}\) contains the frontier shifters, namely the shares of cultivated area under each major crop (crops averaging at least 3% of area, with maize as the base), the survey round and the ecological zone. The two-sided term \(v_{ijt}\) captures noise and shocks outside the operator’s control and is normal with variance \(\sigma_{vj}^{2}\) [48]; the one-sided term \(u_{ijt} \ge 0\) is technical inefficiency. We adopt a half-normal distribution for \(u_{ijt}\), having encountered convergence problems with other distributions in the group-level estimations; exponential, truncated-normal and Rayleigh alternatives are examined among the robustness checks in Section 5.5 (Fig. S2). The inefficiency variance is heteroskedastic, \(\sigma_{u_{ijt}}^{2} = \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})\), where \(w_{ijt}\) contains the operator’s age, schooling and gender, land ownership, mechanization and extension contact, the crop diversification index, fixed effects for ecological zone and survey round, and a constant, following previous work on these data [13], [14], [15], [16]; \(\alpha_{j}\) is estimated separately for each group, so the determinants of inefficiency are themselves allowed to differ between credit users and non-users (Table S4). Credit is excluded from \(w_{ijt}\) because it defines the groups. Table S5 defines every variable entering the frontier, the inefficiency term and the matching distance of Section 4.3, with the unit in which it is measured and the sign expected of it. Given the estimated frontier for group \(j\), the pure technical efficiency of operator \(i\) is the conditional expectation

\[ TE_{ijt} = E\!\left(\exp(-u_{ijt}) \mid \varepsilon_{ijt}\right) \qquad\qquad (2) \]

where \(\varepsilon_{ijt} = v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}\) is the composed error. In the second step, the frontier output predicted for each farmer from its own group frontier, \(\hat{y}_{ijt}\), is pooled across groups and a stochastic metafrontier that envelops the group frontiers is estimated as

\[ f^{M}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(\hat{y}_{ijt}) = \beta_{0M} + \sum_{k} \beta_{kM}\ln(x_{kiMt}) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skM}\ln(x_{kiMt})\ln(x_{siMt}) + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} - u_{Mijt} \qquad\qquad (3) \]

where \(u_{Mijt} \sim N^{+}(0, \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{M}))\) is strictly positive, so that \(f^{j}(x_{ijt}) \le f^{M}(x_{ijt})\) for every group, and the same covariates that scale inefficiency in Equation (1) scale the technology gap. The ratio of group \(j\)’s frontier to the metafrontier is the technology gap ratio,

\[ TGR_{ijt} = \frac{f^{j}(x_{ijt})}{f^{M}(x_{ijt})} = e^{-u_{Mijt}} \le 1 \qquad\qquad (4) \]

and meta-frontier technical efficiency decomposes as

\[ MTE_{ijt} = f^{j}(x_{ijt})\left(f^{M}(x_{ijt})\,e^{v_{ijt}}\right)^{-1} = TGR_{ijt} \times TE_{ijt} \qquad\qquad (5) \]

A TGR below one means that, at the farmer’s input bundle, the group’s technology yields less output than the best practice observed in the pooled sample; a lower TGR is a larger technology gap. TE measures performance against the group’s own frontier and MTE against the common one, so Equation (5) attributes any group difference in MTE to a technology component and an efficiency component, which is the distinction on which H1 and H2 turn: a group can be closer to the metafrontier yet less efficient within its own technology, or the reverse.

Estimation proceeds in the two steps of [46]. First, the group frontiers in Equation (1) are estimated by maximum likelihood on all farmers in each group and TE is obtained from Equation (2). Second, the metafrontier in Equation (3) is estimated by maximum likelihood on the group-frontier predictions, on the matched sample described in Section 4.3 and, for comparison, on the unmatched pooled sample, yielding TGR from Equation (4) and MTE from Equation (5); the enveloping is done by the one-sided term \(u_{Mijt}\) rather than by a programming constraint, so the metafrontier is not forced through the extreme predictions of the group frontiers. Because an unrestricted translog need not satisfy monotonicity and quasi-concavity at every observation, the frontiers are also estimated with these regularity conditions imposed; this restricted specification is the one reported in Table 4 and Tables S3 and S4, Table 4 reports the share of observations at which each estimated frontier satisfies the two conditions, and the unrestricted frontier is carried as a robustness variant (Fig. S2). Input elasticities are the first derivatives of the estimated frontiers with respect to each logged input, evaluated at the sample means, and returns to scale (RTS) are their sum [47]. Group-level TGR, TE and MTE are averages of the farmer-level scores within each group, and the difference between credit users and non-users is estimated directly by the same procedure, with its own standard error, rather than by subtracting two rounded means. Three diagnostics precede interpretation and are reported in Section 5.1: residual-skewness tests [49], [50] and a one-sided likelihood-ratio test [51] establish that a one-sided inefficiency term is present; a likelihood-ratio test of the group frontiers against a common frontier establishes whether the two groups share a technology, which is the condition under which the metafrontier rather than a single frontier is the right benchmark; and the share of composed-error variance attributable to the one-sided term, \(\gamma = \sigma_{u}^{2}/\sigma^{2}\), indicates how much of the unexplained dispersion is systematic.

Two extensions use the same machinery. First, the household credit indicator defines the groups in the preferred specification, and the frontiers are re-estimated under the narrower definitions of Section 2.2, in which the operator alone, the operator’s spouse, or another household member holds the loan, each definition fitted as its own pair of group frontiers, to test whether the results depend on whose borrowing is counted (Table 5). Second, heterogeneity in the credit contrast is examined by computing the credit-minus-no-credit difference in TGR, TE and MTE within subgroups defined by operator gender, age and education (Figure 3), major crop and administrative region (Figure 4), and the financial-service indicators of Section 3, including formal account ownership (Figure 2 and Table 6). These within-subgroup differences are computed from the main estimation’s operator-level scores rather than from separately estimated frontiers, so they describe where the aggregate contrast is concentrated rather than testing distinct technologies within each subgroup.

4.3 Forming comparable pairs of farmers

Three features of the credit indicator could bias a naive comparison of users and non-users: it is self-reported, so recall and social-desirability error can misclassify borrowers; credit is not randomly allocated, so lender targeting and self-selection make borrowers differ from non-borrowers in ways that also affect output; and the treatment can be defined at the household or the operator level. Matching addresses the second of these on observables, the alternative definitions of Section 2.2 address the third, and the first is a measurement problem that no estimator in this paper removes, so we set out its likely direction first.

The classification rests on the household’s own account of a loan application and its outcome, and self-reported borrowing is not a neutral measurement instrument in this setting. Recall over a twelve-month window is imperfect, and the error is unlikely to be random: small and informal loans are the ones most likely to go unreported, and they are disproportionately the loans smallholders take [9], [12]. Reporting may also respond to the interview itself, since having applied and been refused is a less comfortable answer than not having applied. Self-reported financial-access measures of this kind are predictive of the outcomes they are meant to proxy while remaining vulnerable to systematic misreport [1], [2], [42]. If the dominant error is to record genuine borrowers as non-users, the comparison group is contaminated with borrowers and the estimated contrast is attenuated toward zero, so the magnitudes reported in Section 5 would if anything be understated. We do not treat them as formal bounds, because misreporting that is itself correlated with farm performance could move the contrast in either direction and the data offer no way to check.

Credit users are not a random draw of farmers. Table 1 shows that they are younger and better educated than non-users (45.8 against 47.4 years; 6.1 against 4.1 years of schooling), less likely to own their land and more reliant on hired labour, and the loan outcomes in Table 3 indicate that lenders screen on collateral and trust, so borrowing reflects both lender targeting and farmer self-selection. A metafrontier estimated on the raw pooled sample would envelop two groups drawn from different parts of the covariate space, and the resulting technology gap would confound technology with composition. We therefore estimate the metafrontier in Equation (3) on a matched sample in which each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user of similar observed characteristics. The purpose differs from that of matching estimators that impute a missing counterfactual outcome [28], [29]: here the pairs form a balanced sample on which the metafrontier is estimated, while the user/non-user split that defines the group frontiers is preserved, an approach taken by earlier metafrontier studies facing similar selection concerns [31], [32], [33], [52], [53]. Pairs are formed only within exact strata of operator gender, survey round, region, ecological zone and rural or urban locality, so that no user is compared with a non-user from a different round, place or gender. Within a stratum, the distance between candidates is computed over the operator’s demographics (age, schooling, marital status, religion, ethnicity and relationship to the household head), household composition (size, dependency ratio and female share), production choices (crop diversification and the share of land under each crop), land ownership, and the financial-inclusion index described in Section 2.3, whose indicator set, stratum-specific estimation and rescaling onto a common metric are documented in Note S1. Including the index is deliberate: it means that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services, so that the credit contrast is not a proxy for being banked or insured, dimensions that re-enter as heterogeneity cuts in Figure 2 and Table 6. Observations missing any matching covariate are excluded before pairing, and because matching is one-to-one, the matched sample contains equal numbers of users and non-users and is a small fraction of the pooled sample; the group frontiers in Table 4 are estimated on all users and all non-users, with matching applied at the metafrontier stage, so the resulting contrast describes households that resemble borrowers on the matched characteristics rather than the average non-borrowing farm.

Because the covariates are numerous and of mixed type, we compute the distance under eight metrics: propensity scores from logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit models, Euclidean and scaled Euclidean distance, and Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance [54], [55]. Comparing them is not incidental to the design. The model used for the propensity score, the distance metric and the rule that forms the pairs are implementation choices to which a matching estimate is sensitive, and the practical guidance is to settle them on the balance achieved after matching rather than on the estimates they produce [56]. Balance is assessed for every covariate by the absolute standardized mean difference, the variance ratio and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, whose targets are zero, one and zero respectively [30], [57], and the specifications are ranked on a composite of these diagnostics rather than on the frontier results they yield. Fig. S1 reports all three for each matched sample against the unmatched sample. Every matched sample removes most of the imbalance visible in the unmatched sample, which is concentrated in schooling, household size, the crop-share indicators and the ethnic, religious and regional composition of the two groups; residual imbalance after matching is largest for household size and operator age and is reported rather than assumed away. The probit propensity-score specification ranks best on the composite criterion and provides the matched sample used in the main analysis; Section 5.5 reports the estimates under each of the other seven matched samples and under no matching (Fig. S2).

The matched sample also supports a direct comparison of input use that precedes the frontier results. For each of the six frontier inputs, expressed per hectare, and for the real value of output per hectare, we estimate the proportional gap associated with credit as a log-linear treatment effect on the matched pairs, for the matched sample as a whole and separately over the covariate distributions of non-users and of users, with the same jackknife inference as the frontier estimates (Figure 1). These gaps are the input-intensity counterpart of the frontier comparison: the frontiers say how much output a group’s technology yields from a given bundle, and Figure 1 says whether credit users in fact apply a different bundle, so that a contrast arising because borrowers operate a different technology can be distinguished from one arising because they use more or less of the same inputs.

4.4 What the design identifies

Matching balances the covariates we observe. It cannot balance what the GLSS does not record, and several of the omitted determinants of both borrowing and farm performance are plausibly correlated with one another: managerial ability, risk tolerance [11], the quality and provenance of the land the household farms, wealth held outside the surveyed asset modules, prior relationships with lenders, and standing in the community associations through which group-based lending is intermediated. The last of these is not a remote concern here: as Table 3 shows, group-based microfinance rose from 23.8% to 39.2% of loans between the two rounds, so the mechanism allocating credit is increasingly one whose inputs we do not observe. Selectivity-corrected frontier models could in principle address this, but they require an exclusion restriction, a variable that predicts household borrowing and is credibly unrelated to farm performance, and the GLSS contains none that we are prepared to defend; we do not construct one.

We therefore interpret the estimated differences in TGR, TE and MTE as associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as causal effects of credit. Where Section 5 uses the language of gaps, differentials or influence, it should be read in that sense. The direction of any remaining bias is not signed by theory: if lenders select the more capable farmers, or the more capable farmers are those who seek credit, the observed contrasts overstate what credit does for the marginal borrower; if borrowing is concentrated among households under financial stress or diversifying out of farming, they understate it. This matters for how the hypotheses are adjudicated. A rejection of H1 is evidence that borrowing households do not, as a group, operate the best-practice technology; it does not by itself establish that borrowing moved them away from it. Two exhibits speak to the question without resolving it. Table 5 re-estimates the contrast under narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed, and a contrast that is stable across the operator’s own loan, a spouse’s loan and another member’s loan is harder to attribute to operator-specific unobservables. The loan-application row of Table 6 estimates the contrast within households in which the operator applied for a loan, so that credit users are compared with applicants whose household did not obtain one; this is the nearest the data come to a comparison in which demand is held constant, although refusal is itself a lender’s judgement and the unfunded comparison group is small.

Three further limits bound the interpretation. First, credit is measured as an indicator of use rather than of access: a household that could borrow on good terms and chose not to is pooled with one that could not borrow at all, so the contrast is between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained. That the modal reason for not applying is “no need” rather than an institutional barrier, at 55.4% and 63.7% of non-applicants in the two rounds (Table 3), makes the distinction material, and so does the fact that only 29.0% of loans in 2012/13 were reported as taken for farming: a household counted as a credit user may have borrowed for a purpose that never touched the farm, and the group frontiers characterize the technology of borrowing households whatever the loan was used for. It is also one reason the gaps here need not match those in studies that classify households by a direct elicitation of credit constraints [9], [10]. Second, the design assumes no interference between units, which is not innocuous when a substantial and rising share of lending is group-based and intermediated through the same communities that supply the comparison group; expanded lending to one household may alter the terms available to its neighbours, in either direction, and theory does not determine the direction of the resulting bias. Third, the data are repeated cross-sections, so the estimates compare households at a point in time rather than tracking the same farm before and after borrowing, and the two rounds describe how the associations differ between 2012/13 and 2016/17, not how any farm’s performance changed when it obtained credit; the heterogeneity reported in Section 5.6 is obtained by summarizing the matched-sample scores within subgroups, and those contrasts are descriptive rather than separately identified effects.

4.5 Inference and robustness

Standard errors come from a cluster jackknife at the enumeration-area (EA) level, the primary sampling unit of the GLSS. For each survey round we form 100 delete-one-EA replicates; in each replicate one EA is removed, the remaining EAs from both rounds are pooled, and the full pipeline is re-run: the group frontiers in Equation (1) are re-estimated with the regularity conditions imposed, the matching is redone, the metafrontier in Equation (3) is re-estimated, and TE, TGR, MTE, the elasticities, the input and output gaps and the subgroup differences are recomputed. Jackknife standard errors are the dispersion of the replicate estimates, so a single set of standard errors carries the uncertainty from clustered sampling, from matching and from frontier estimation together rather than treating the matched sample as fixed.
