Because the credit-minus-no-credit differences are recomputed within each replicate, each difference in Tables 4 to 6 and in the figures carries its own jackknife standard error rather than one assembled from the two group estimates. We report two-sided tests on these standard errors, mark significance at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels in the tables, and use the 5% level as the threshold in the text, distinguishing throughout the statistical significance of a difference from its economic size.

Robustness is assessed on the same footing and is organized around the sources of specification dependence identified above. Table 5 re-estimates the contrasts under alternative definitions of which household member holds the credit. Fig. S2 re-estimates the headline TGR, TE and MTE contrasts along six dimensions: the functional form (translog against Cobb-Douglas); the distribution of the inefficiency term (half-normal against exponential, truncated-normal and Rayleigh); the estimator used to recover farmer-level efficiency from the composed error; the aggregation of farmer-level scores into group means (weighted mean, simple mean and median); the matched sample (each of the eight distance metrics and the unmatched sample); and the regularity restrictions (restricted against unrestricted frontiers). Section 5.5 reports which of these choices move the estimates and by how much, and a finding is described as robust only along the dimensions on which it survives.

5. Results and discussion

This section reports what the matched meta-stochastic frontier reveals about crop production in households that used credit relative to matched households that did not, and interprets the estimates against the hypotheses of Section 4.1 and the financing environment of Section 3. Section 5.1 presents the diagnostics that justify the frontier specification and the separation of the two groups’ technologies. Section 5.2 compares input elasticities and returns to scale across the naive, group and metafrontiers, which speaks to H3. Section 5.3 carries the paper’s central result, the decomposition of the credit contrast into a technology gap and a technical-efficiency gap, together with what matching changes and what the matched input and output gaps of Figure 1 add. Because the central result runs against H1, Section 5.4 weighs the readings of it that the data can and cannot support. Section 5.5 tests whether the decomposition survives alternative treatment definitions, matched samples and frontier specifications, and Section 5.6 asks for whom, for which crops and where the gaps are concentrated. Unless stated otherwise, estimates refer to the household credit definition on the one-to-one matched sample, a translog frontier with a half-normal inefficiency term and the regularity restrictions imposed, with jackknife standard errors from 100 delete-one-enumeration-area replicates. Every difference is reported as credit users less non-users, and every difference is an association conditional on observables in a balanced sample, in the sense set out in Section 4.4.

5.1 Diagnostic tests

Table 4 reports the diagnostics for the five frontiers estimated: the naive national frontier, the two group frontiers for non-users [A] and credit users [B], and the metafrontier on the matched and unmatched samples. The first question is whether a one-sided inefficiency component belongs in the error at all. The residual-skewness statistics of [49] and [50] are negative for every frontier, as a one-sided term in a production frontier implies, the Coelli statistic ranging from -3.21 for the credit-user frontier to -99.39 for the unmatched metafrontier, and the boundary likelihood-ratio test of [51] rejects the null of no inefficiency in each case, with statistics of 1,466.2 and 145.6 for the non-user and credit-user frontiers and 562.3 for the matched metafrontier. Deviations from the frontier are therefore not attributable to symmetric noise alone, and a stochastic frontier rather than an average-response production function is the appropriate description of the data.

The second question is whether credit users and non-users can be assessed against a single frontier. The metafrontier likelihood-ratio test rejects a common technology in both samples, with statistics of 5,095 on the matched sample and 46,613 on the unmatched sample, far above any conventional critical value. The two groups produce under different technologies, so their performance has to be decomposed into how well each group uses its own technology and how far that technology sits from best practice, which is what Equations (4) and (5) do; comparing the groups through a single pooled efficiency score would conflate the two, which is the confounding that metafrontier applications to Ghanaian agriculture have been designed to avoid [13], [14], [15], [16].

The third set of diagnostics concerns regularity and the composition of the error. At the observation level the single frontiers are only partly well behaved: monotonicity holds for 49% of observations under the naive frontier and for 75% and 61% under the non-user and credit-user frontiers, and curvature for only 22%, 21% and 26% respectively, although every elasticity is positive at the sample means at which it is evaluated, so the models are well behaved on average even where individual observations violate the conditions. The regularity-restricted metafrontier does what it is meant to do: monotonicity is satisfied for 100% of observations in both the matched and the unmatched metafrontier, and curvature for 93% of observations in the matched metafrontier against 58% in the unmatched one. The matched metafrontier is therefore the specification on which the elasticities and technology gaps below can be read with the least concern about local violations of economic regularity, which is one reason, alongside covariate balance, for treating the matched estimates as the preferred ones. The share of composed-error variance attributable to the one-sided term, \(\gamma = \sigma_{u}^{2}/\sigma^{2}\), is 0.600 in the non-user frontier and 0.670 in the credit-user frontier, so within each group the dominant source of unexplained dispersion is inefficiency rather than noise; in the metafrontier, where the one-sided term is the technology gap, the share is 0.867 on the matched sample against 0.694 on the unmatched one, so most of the distance between the group frontiers and the envelope is systematic rather than idiosyncratic. Both margins matter, which is the premise on which the metafrontier design rests.

5.2 Output elasticities and returns to scale

Table 4 reports input elasticities evaluated at the sample means, with the underlying translog coefficients in Table S3. Under the naive national frontier every input has a positive elasticity that is significant at the 1% level, consistent with earlier frontier estimates for Ghanaian crop production on these data [13], [14], [15], [16]. Land dominates, with an elasticity of 0.763, followed by family labour (0.150), planting material (0.051), pesticide (0.026), hired labour (0.021) and fertilizer (0.014). Returns to scale are 1.024, marginally above constant. The ordering is the familiar one for Ghanaian smallholders, whose output responds overwhelmingly to the extensive margin and to household labour and only modestly to purchased inputs.

The group frontiers speak to H3, and the evidence is narrower than the hypothesis anticipated. Because the jackknife standard errors are small, most differences in the [B−A] column are statistically significant, and it is their magnitude that carries the economic content. On that criterion one input stands out. The family-labour elasticity is 0.197 for credit users against 0.147 for non-users, a difference of 0.049 that is significant at the 1% level, about a third of the non-user elasticity, and accounts for almost the whole of the returns-to-scale gap (1.074 against 1.021, a difference of 0.052). The land elasticity is identical across groups to three decimals (0.762 and 0.762), so credit is not associated with higher returns at the extensive margin. The fertilizer elasticity is slightly higher for credit users (0.018 against 0.013), which runs opposite to the sign H3 posited, hired labour is higher by 0.001, and planting material and pesticide are lower by 0.001 and 0.002; each of these differences is below one percentage point of output and none would change the ranking of inputs within either group. H3 is thus supported for family labour and not for land, and the fertilizer elasticity moves in the wrong direction by an amount too small to bear interpretation, from a base that is small for both groups. That fertilizer margin is worth a further word, because a leading account of low fertilizer use in African agriculture attributes it to uninsured risk acting together with the absence of credit rather than to either alone: in Ethiopia, households more exposed to a shortfall in consumption after a bad harvest applied less fertilizer, so that risk and the inability to borrow against the outlay reinforced one another [11]. If that account carried over to the population studied here, households whose credit constraint is the less binding of the two would show a distinctly different fertilizer regime from comparable non-borrowers. They do not. The two group frontiers differ on fertilizer by an amount too small to interpret, the higher of the two elasticities being the credit users’ rather than the non-users’, and the quantity of fertilizer actually applied, taken up with Figure 1 in Section 5.3, is lower among borrowers than among their matched comparators. Neither margin is what that account would predict, so the Ethiopian evidence stands as a contrast to what these data show rather than a confirmation of it, and the contrast is one more reason to ask, as Section 5.4 does, whether the borrowing recorded here is the kind that finances fertilizer at all. The credit-user technology is not more input-responsive across the board; it is more responsive to household labour, at the same returns to land and with mildly increasing rather than constant returns to scale.

Two readings of the family-labour result are consistent with the data, and the design cannot separate them. One is that credit-using households deploy their own labour more productively at the margin, for instance through better timing of operations that liquidity makes possible; an elasticity describes the curvature of a group’s frontier at its mean input bundle, so a higher family-labour elasticity is consistent with those farms operating where additional household labour still adds substantially to output, particularly if, as Figure 1 shows below, they combine it with fewer purchased inputs. The other is compositional: the group frontier is fitted on the borrowing households as they are, and a frontier fitted on a younger, more educated group can display a higher family-labour elasticity without any change in how a given household farms. Table S3 adds one feature worth carrying forward to the heterogeneity results. The coefficient on the cocoa area share is positive in every frontier and much larger in the credit-user frontier (0.677) than in the non-user frontier (0.186), so the technology credit users operate is relatively favourable to cocoa even though, as shown below, it is less favourable to most other crops.

The last two columns of Table 4 give the metafrontier elasticities on the matched and unmatched samples. The two are close and preserve the same ranking of inputs: land is 0.748 matched against 0.754 unmatched, family labour 0.155 against 0.144, planting material 0.045 against 0.051, pesticide 0.031 against 0.025, and returns to scale 1.019 against 1.013, with hired labour and fertilizer coinciding to within a thousandth. Balancing the sample therefore changes the shape of the envelope only modestly; its main effect, shown next, is on the position of the two groups relative to it. What the elasticities establish is that the best-practice technology, like both group technologies, is land-intensive with near-constant returns to scale, so the technology gaps discussed next are gaps in the level of the frontier rather than in its shape.

5.3 Technology gaps, technical efficiency and meta-frontier efficiency

Table 4 decomposes performance into the technology gap ratio of Equation (4), pure technical efficiency from Equation (2) and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency, from Equation (5); the Matched rows are the preferred estimates and the Unmatched rows show what balancing the sample changes. Table 5 repeats the matched comparison for the household definition alongside the narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed, which Section 5.5 takes up.

The technology gap is the headline result, and it runs against H1. In the matched sample the mean TGR is 0.929 for non-users and 0.877 for credit users: the technology set operated by non-users produces, on average, 93% of the output attainable under the best-practice technology at the same inputs, and that of credit users 88%. The difference of 5.3 percentage points is significant at the 1% level, is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5, and is negative. Section 4.1 hypothesized the opposite on the grounds that credit finances the lumpy investments that move a farm toward best practice. In these data borrowing households are not, as a group, operating the best-practice technology; their frontier lies farther inside the metafrontier than the frontier of comparable non-users, and matching on gender, round, region, agro-ecology, locality and a rich set of household, farm and financial-inclusion covariates does not remove that difference. The unmatched gap is of the same sign and similar size (6.0 percentage points), so the finding is not created by matching either.

Pure technical efficiency, which measures each group against its own frontier, differs little between the groups, and the sign of the small difference is not stable across specifications. Table 4, built from the regularity-restricted frontiers, gives mean TE of 0.633 for non-users and 0.635 for credit users, a difference of 0.3 percentage points in favour of credit users; Table 5, built from the unrestricted frontiers, gives 0.640 and 0.626 for the same definition, a difference of 1.4 points against them, and Section 5.5 shows that the sign also moves across matched samples and aggregation rules. Both differences are statistically significant because the jackknife standard errors are small, but a gap that changes sign with the regularity restrictions imposed on the frontier, and that stays within about two percentage points of zero under every specification examined, is not a gap on which an interpretation should rest. The defensible statement is that, relative to their own technology, credit users and matched non-users are about equally efficient, each attaining roughly 63% of their own frontier output, a level of within-technology inefficiency in line with earlier Ghanaian frontier studies [13], [15], [16]. H2, which predicted lower efficiency among credit users, receives at most weak support, and we do not read the data as establishing an efficiency penalty of borrowing.

Because the efficiency margin is close to neutral, the meta-frontier efficiency gap is the technology gap. Matched MTE is 0.588 for non-users and 0.559 for credit users in Table 4, a statistically significant shortfall of 2.9 percentage points, and 0.595 against 0.552 in Table 5, a shortfall of 4.3 points. Whichever specification is preferred, the MTE gap is negative, significant and of the same order as the TGR gap, so the shortfall of credit-using households relative to best practice is a technology gap and not an efficiency gap. Both groups, it should be stressed, operate well inside the metafrontier, at about 59% and 56% of attainable output; the credit gap is a modest increment on a large common shortfall of the kind widely documented for African smallholders [6], [13], and the economically relevant statement is not that borrowers farm worse but that the technology they farm with is, on average, farther from the best available, by an amount several times the efficiency difference in either direction. The attribution differs from the one [13] report across agro-ecologies, where technical inefficiency outweighs technology differences. The two results are not in conflict, because they decompose different contrasts, but together they caution against assuming that any production shortfall in Ghana is a management problem.

The comparison between the matched and unmatched rows of Table 4 shows what matching does to these contrasts, and it is the most informative feature of the table. In the unmatched sample credit users trail non-users by 7.9 percentage points in TE and 11.2 points in MTE, several times the matched values, whereas the unmatched TGR gap is close to the matched one. Balancing the two groups on observables therefore removes almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and most of the raw MTE deficit, but leaves the technology gap essentially intact. The raw efficiency deficit was compositional, a statement about who borrows on the dimensions Section 4.3 balances; the technology gap survives the comparison of like with like. Observable selection into borrowing explains the efficiency difference and almost none of the technology difference.

Figure 1 places the frontier results beside the input and output levels of the matched pairs. It reports, for the matched sample, the proportional gap associated with credit in each per-hectare input and in the real value of output per hectare, evaluated for the sample as a whole and with reference to the non-user and user subsamples. Credit-using households apply substantially less fertilizer, planting material, hired labour and pesticide per hectare than their matched comparators, the fertilizer gap being the largest and each of the four gaps significant at the 1% level; land area, against which the other inputs are normalized, registers no gap; household labour does not differ significantly; and the value of output per hectare is slightly higher for credit users, a difference that does not reach the 5% level. The three reference populations give nearly identical gaps, so the pattern does not depend on which group’s covariate distribution is used. Two things follow. First, the hired-labour advantage of borrowing households in the unmatched data of Table 1 (25 against 19 man-days per hectare) does not survive comparison with observably similar non-borrowers; it reflected who borrows rather than what borrowing finances. Second, credit is not associated with intensification on the purchased-input margin in these data, which is the opposite of what a liquidity-relaxing account of credit predicts. Read with Table 4, the picture is of a borrowing group whose technology relies more on land and household labour and less on purchased inputs, lies inside the best-practice envelope, produces about as much per hectare as the comparison group, and is run about as efficiently, relative to that technology, as the comparison group runs its own. The lower TGR of credit users therefore cannot be read as borrowed money buying inputs that fail to raise output; it is the technology in use, evaluated at common input levels, that sits farther from best practice.

5.4 Interpreting the negative technology gap

The technology gap is measured against a metafrontier that envelops both group frontiers, so a lower TGR for credit users says that the technology of borrowing households, as a group, is not the best practice in the sample. It does not say what makes it so, and Section 4.4 rules out a causal reading. Four readings are consistent with the evidence of Sections 2, 3 and 5.3, and the data discriminate among them only partially.

The first is loan use. Household credit relaxes the household’s liquidity constraint, not the farm’s, and the loan-purpose codes of Table 3 show that agriculture is a minority use of it: in 2012/13, the round in which the recorded purposes exhaust the loans, only 29.0% were taken for agricultural purposes, the remainder financing business, education, ceremonies, debt repayment and other household needs. Fungibility of agricultural credit within the household is well documented [26], and Figure 1 is what fungibility looks like on the farm: borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs. On this reading the negative technology gap is not a failure of credit to reach the farm so much as evidence that, for most of these households, the loan was never directed there, and the household indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. This is the reading the exhibits most directly support, and it is consistent with the northern-Ghana finding that even input-linked credit raised input use without proportionate output gains [20]; the survey records the stated purpose of a loan but not the use of each cedi, so it cannot be confirmed at the level of the individual farm.

The second is selection on what the GLSS does not record. Matching balances the covariates in Table 1 and Fig. S1, but not the reasons a household applies for a loan and a lender grants it. Distress borrowing after a shock, borrowing to fund a non-farm enterprise, and lender targeting of households with particular repayment prospects would each place borrowers on a different technology for reasons the design cannot see, and the growing share of group-based microfinance in Table 3, from 23.8% to 39.2% of loans, means that allocation increasingly runs through community institutions whose membership the GLSS does not observe. Differences in risk preference that affect both borrowing and technology choice belong here too [11]. The stability of the TGR gap between the unmatched and matched samples is consistent with this reading, since it shows that the gap is orthogonal to the observables the matching uses; it cannot show whether the gap is orthogonal to what the matching does not use, and the direction of the resulting bias is not signed.

The third is the distinction between use and access. The treatment is an indicator of having borrowed, and the modal reason for not applying is having no need for a loan (55.4% and 63.7% of non-applicants in the two rounds, Table 3), so the comparison group mixes households that are credit constrained with a larger number that, on their own account, are not. The literature that finds credit constraints lowering farm productivity identifies the constrained explicitly [9], [10], [44]; the contrast estimated here is a different object, and a negative gap for borrowers against a largely unconstrained comparison group is not in tension with it. If the households that choose not to borrow are, on average, the ones already operating the better technology, the estimated gap partly reflects that sorting. Table 6 offers a partial check. Within households in which the operator applied for a loan, a subgroup in which demand is held constant, the TGR contrast between credit users and applicants whose household did not obtain credit is -6.1 percentage points, close to the full-sample gap, so the headline gap is not an artefact of comparing applicants with non-applicants; the TE and MTE contrasts in that row are larger, but the unfunded comparison group is small and is selected by lenders’ decisions, so we do not lean on them. Experimental evidence from Ghana approaches the same distinction from the supply side. Offering maize farmers in the north rainfall-index insurance and cash grants in varying combinations, [19] find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of the risk constraint and changed little when capital alone was supplied, which places the binding constraint for that population in uninsured risk rather than in liquidity. On that evidence a negative technology gap among borrowers is not in itself surprising, because relaxing a credit constraint need not move a farm’s technology when risk is what binds, and the near-absence of cover against production risk documented in Section 3 is part of the environment in which the loans observed here were taken. The experiment does not, however, settle the reading of the contrast estimated here: it supplied capital to farmers who did not have to seek it, in one crop and one region, so it speaks to access where this treatment records use, and it identifies which constraint binds where this design can only describe the households in which borrowing is observed.

The fourth is measurement. Section 4.3 argues that self-reported borrowing under-records small and informal loans, which would place some genuine borrowers in the comparison group and attenuate the contrast toward zero. Attenuation does not generate a negative gap; it makes the estimated gap, if anything, an understatement of the true difference in absolute value. It cannot explain the sign.

What the data cannot do is assign weights to these readings. The GLSS records the purpose of a loan but not what the household did with the liquidity it freed, records that a loan was granted but not why, and records use rather than access. The disaggregations of Section 5.6 narrow the space somewhat, because the technology gap is present in every financial-service subgroup and every region, which is difficult to reconcile with a story confined to one lending channel or one agro-ecology. The honest summary is that the negative technology gap is a robust description of Ghanaian borrowing households, not an estimate of what credit does to a farm.

Placed against the Ghanaian literature, the result reconciles rather than contradicts. Positive credit-efficiency associations have been reported for maize producers under programme and input-linked financing [22], [24], no association for rice under bank-linked credit [21], modest output effects of input credit [20], and financial inclusion more broadly has been linked to smallholder productivity [25]. Those studies observe credit tied to farm inputs, or crops and regions in which such credit predominates, and they compare borrowers and non-borrowers on a single frontier; the estimates here are national in scope, net of matching on observables, and drawn from a population in which little household borrowing is agricultural. The nationally representative decomposition therefore does not show that agricultural credit fails to move farms toward the frontier; it shows that credit as households actually obtain and use it is not associated with best-practice technology and does not raise or lower within-technology efficiency in any robust way. The distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper’s substantive contribution to that literature.

Table S4 adds covariate detail that points the same way. In the matched metafrontier, whose one-sided term is the technology gap, the gap is larger for female-operated farms (coefficient 0.583) and smaller where the household owns its land (-0.442), uses mechanized equipment (-0.272), receives extension advice (-0.296) or grows a more diversified crop mix (-0.308), all significant at the 1% level, while years of schooling carries a small positive coefficient (0.036), meaning a larger distance from best practice. Distance from best practice is thus associated with the same tenure, service and gender factors that structure technology access in Ghanaian agriculture generally [15], [16], not with the borrowing indicator that defines the groups.

The policy reading follows from which channel carries the gap. A shortfall located in technical efficiency would call for managerial support through extension, training and record-keeping bundled with the loan; the evidence does not support that diagnosis, because the efficiency difference is small, of unstable sign, and disappears once borrowers are compared with similar non-borrowers. A shortfall located in the technology gap calls for changing the technology farms can obtain and use, but here the gap is not the technology gap that input-constrained farms display, because credit users apply fewer purchased inputs rather than more, and it appears alongside loans that are mostly not used on the farm. The finding therefore does not support expanding household credit as such as an instrument for closing Ghana’s crop technology gap, and it does not support the opposite proposition either, since the design cannot establish what credit does to a given farm. It is consistent with the view, long argued for agricultural finance in sub-Saharan Africa, that finance moves technology only when it is designed around the farm’s investment and timing needs and bundled with the inputs, information and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking [12], [34], and with demand-side accounts in which low uptake reflects the limited value farmers see in the products on offer [27]. The bundling argument is consistent with these findings, but it is not tested by them; Section 6 draws out the implications after the robustness and heterogeneity evidence has been presented.

5.5 Robustness of the main findings

Three features of the main result need to survive scrutiny: the sign and size of the TGR gap, the smallness of the TE gap, and the consequent attribution of the MTE gap to technology. Efficiency scores are not specification-free. The inputs entered, the functional form, the distribution assumed for the one-sided term and the estimator used to recover producer-level scores can each move mean efficiency and the ranking of producers within the same data [58], so no single specification can establish the size, and still less the sign, of a difference between two groups’ scores; the spread of estimates across defensible specifications is itself the evidence, and we read it that way rather than selecting the specification that gives the cleanest answer. We examine each of the three features across the definition of treatment, the matched sample and the frontier specification, and the exercise separates them rather than confirming them together: the technology component holds its sign and its size throughout, while the efficiency component does not.

Table 5 varies whose borrowing defines the household as a credit user; each definition is fitted as its own pair of frontiers, so the non-user column varies across rows. The technology gap is negative and significant at the 1% level under every definition, and larger under the narrower ones: 5.3 percentage points for household credit, 9.2 points for the operator’s own credit, 11.3 points for spousal credit and 8.9 points for credit held by another member. The household definition, being the broadest, gives the smallest gap, so the preferred estimate is if anything the conservative one, and the operator-only definition promised in Section 2.2 reproduces the headline result with a larger magnitude. The TE difference is small under every definition but not of one sign: it runs against credit users by 2.5 points under the operator-only definition and by 2.5 points under the other-member definition, but in their favour, by 3.6 points, when the spouse holds the loan. The MTE gap is negative throughout, from 3.0 points under spousal credit to 6.6 points under the operator-only definition, and in each case the technology gap is the larger component. Whose borrowing is counted changes the size of the shortfall and the sign of its small efficiency component; it does not change the direction of the technology gap or of overall performance, and a contrast that holds for the operator’s own loan, a spouse’s loan and another member’s loan is harder to attribute to operator-specific unobservables.

Fig. S1 reports covariate balance for the unmatched sample and for each of the eight matched samples described in Section 4.3, on absolute standardized mean differences, variance ratios and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The unmatched sample is most imbalanced on schooling, household size and several crop-share, ethnicity and regional indicators. Every matched sample brings the standardized differences and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics close to zero on nearly all covariates, the propensity-score and robust Mahalanobis schemes bring the variance ratios closest to one, and the differences among the propensity-score schemes are small, so the choice among them is not consequential for balance; the probit propensity-score sample, which the composite ranking selects, underlies Tables 4 to 6 and Figures 1 to 4. Two covariates deserve mention. Household size is the one covariate on which a standardized difference of moderate size survives in every matched sample, and the propensity-score matches leave a moderate difference in operator age that the distance-based matches remove, so balance on those dimensions is imperfect; given the family-labour result of Section 5.2, this is a further reason not to over-read the small TE gap.

Fig. S2 re-estimates the three gaps under the alternative specifications listed in Section 4.5, with the preferred estimate marked as a reference band. Across the eight matched samples, formed on Euclidean, scaled Euclidean, Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance and on logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit propensity scores, the TGR gap is negative and of similar size in every case, the MTE gap is negative in every case, and the TE gap moves on both sides of zero within a narrow band. The unmatched sample stands apart with a far larger negative TE and MTE gap and a TGR gap close to the matched ones, which repeats the lesson of Table 4. Replacing the translog with a Cobb-Douglas frontier, computing scores by the Jondrow-type or the conditional-model estimator rather than the Battese-Coelli estimator, and aggregating operator-level scores by the simple mean or the median rather than the weighted mean all leave the TGR and MTE gaps negative and close to the preferred estimate, while the TE gap again changes sign across these choices. Lifting the regularity restrictions leaves the TGR gap identical and moves only the TE and MTE gaps, both of which become more negative under the unrestricted frontier; this is the same restricted-against-unrestricted difference that separates Table 4 from Table 5, and it is why the paper treats the TGR gap as the robust finding and the sign of the TE gap as unresolved.

The distributional checks are the least reassuring and deserve to be stated plainly. The exponential distribution for the one-sided term reproduces the ordering with a considerably larger negative TGR gap and a positive TE gap. The Rayleigh and truncated-normal variants returned point estimates without jackknife standard errors, and for those variants the TGR gap is close to zero or of the opposite sign; the truncated-normal variant returned a technology-gap estimate only. We draw no inference from them, and they mark the limit of the claim. The half-normal baseline is retained because it is the specification that estimates on every subsample and replicate, and the finding that credit users sit farther below the metafrontier is established under the half-normal and exponential distributions and under every treatment-definition, functional-form, estimator, aggregation, matching and regularity variant, but it is not established under every distributional assumption, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Taken together, the robustness exercise ranks the three findings by their stability: the negative technology gap is robust to the definition of credit, the functional form, the efficiency estimator, the aggregation rule, the matching scheme and the regularity restrictions; the negative MTE gap is robust in sign and moderately sensitive in magnitude; and the TE gap is small under every specification and its sign is not identified by these data.

5.6 Heterogeneity across financial-service use, farmers, crops and regions

The gaps reported so far average over households that differ in their other financial services, their characteristics, their crops and their locations. This subsection asks where the technology gap and the efficiency gap are concentrated. The disaggregated estimates summarize the operator-level TGR, TE and MTE from the single matched metafrontier within each subgroup; the frontiers are not re-estimated by subgroup, so the estimates describe heterogeneity within the main result rather than separate models, and the same associational reading applies. In Table 6 each cell is the credit-user mean less the non-user mean within the stated group.

Figure 2 and Table 6 examine the contrast across financial-service use, which is where the paper’s framing in terms of financial inclusion rather than credit alone is tested; no exhibit reports the decomposition by the financial-inclusion index, which enters the analysis as a matching covariate rather than as a stratifier and whose construction is documented in Note S1. The technology gap is negative and significant within every financial-service subgroup the GLSS allows: -5.6 percentage points among households with a formal account, -5.2 among the insured, and, across institution types, from -4.7 points among mobile-money users to -9.5 among the small group holding an investment or mortgage account, with bank customers, savings-and-loans and susu scheme members and cooperative or credit-union members all in the same range. There is no financial-service configuration in the data within which borrowing households operate the best-practice technology, and holding another financial product does not narrow the technology gap of credit users. Where account ownership matters is on the efficiency margin. Figure 2 shows that among households without a formal account the TE contrast favours credit users and offsets most of the technology gap, so that the MTE gap is close to zero, whereas among account holders the TE contrast is negative and the MTE gap is clearly negative and at least as large as the aggregate gap of Table 4. The shortfall in meta-frontier efficiency associated with credit is therefore concentrated among the formally included, which is the opposite of the complementarity between credit and account ownership that the financial-inclusion literature anticipates [1], [25]. Institution type matters in the same way: the TE contrast is strongly negative among susu-scheme participants (-9.7 points), whose MTE gap of -12.1 points is the largest among the institution types, and among customers of commercial, community and rural banks (-4.7 points); it is indistinguishable from zero among mobile-money users; and it is positive among members of cooperatives and credit unions (8.6 points), for whom the efficiency advantage is large enough that credit users outperform matched non-users against the metafrontier by 5.4 points. Membership-based institutions that combine credit with savings discipline and peer information are thus the one channel in which credit use coincides with better within-technology performance, in line with evidence that savings groups change household financial behaviour more than they change income [42], although the subgroup is small. The data cannot say whether these patterns reflect the kind of credit that account holders and scheme members obtain, the kind of household that holds an account, or the uses to which account-holding households put liquidity; read with the loan-purpose evidence of Table 3, they are consistent with borrowing among the formally included being directed to non-farm uses to a greater extent than borrowing among the unbanked, but the survey does not link loan purpose to the farm-level scores and this remains a conjecture. A decomposition of the credit contrast by the source of the loan and by its reported purpose, the two dimensions Table 3 records and that no current exhibit crosses with the operator-level scores, would test that conjecture directly; it is not available here, and we identify it as the cut the evidence most needs rather than anticipate what it would show. The source-of-information block of Table 6 is reported for completeness and not interpreted, because its category labels do not map consistently onto the corresponding block of Table 2 read in Section 3, and the reasons-for-no-account block, whose category indicators rest on the same response-coding mechanism, is likewise left uninterpreted.

Figure 3 disaggregates by operator gender, age and education. The technology gap is negative and significant in every group, so no demographic group of credit users operates a technology closer to best practice than its matched non-users. The gap is wider for female than for male operators, which is consistent with the larger technology gap for female-operated farms in Table S4 and with the gender gaps in technology use documented on the same data [15]; it narrows steadily with operator age; and it is not monotone in schooling, being smallest for operators with no formal education and larger at every level of schooling. The efficiency contrast is small, within about two percentage points, for every group but one: it favours credit users among female operators, operators under sixty and those with no formal, primary or senior secondary schooling, is negligible for men, runs against credit users for the oldest operators, and is strongly negative for the small group educated beyond senior secondary level, for whom credit users are markedly less efficient within their own technology. The MTE gap is negative in every group, smallest for operators with senior secondary schooling and with no formal education, where an efficiency advantage offsets part of the technology gap, and largest by a wide margin for the post-secondary group, where the two margins compound. The expectation that better-educated, prime-age male operators would convert credit into technology gains more readily is not borne out; the technology gap is broad-based, and where the credit contrast is least adverse it is because of an efficiency offset, not a smaller technology gap.

Figure 4 disaggregates by major crop and by administrative region. Across crops the technology gap is negative for nine of the eleven crops shown, largest for pepper, maize, cassava and rice and smallest for millet, plantain and yam; it is indistinguishable from zero for sorghum and positive, though small, only for cocoa, the one crop for which credit-using households operate a technology closer to best practice than their matched non-users. The cocoa exception is consistent with the large cocoa-share coefficient in the credit-user frontier noted in Section 5.2, and cocoa is also the one export crop, with sector-specific input and extension arrangements of its own [45], but whether the exception reflects those arrangements or the selection of better-endowed households into cocoa borrowing cannot be established from the survey, which does not record loan purpose by crop. The efficiency contrasts by crop are small and of mixed sign, favouring credit users for plantain, groundnut, maize, rice and cassava, running against them for pepper, cocoa and yam, and not significant for millet, beans and sorghum, so the MTE gap is negative for most crops, widest for pepper, rice, millet, beans and maize, indistinguishable from zero for sorghum and cocoa, and positive only for plantain, where a large efficiency advantage outweighs a moderate technology gap. Across regions the technology gap is negative in all ten, widest in Volta and Greater Accra and narrowest in Northern and Western regions; the efficiency contrast is essentially zero in the three northern regions and in Greater Accra, favours credit users in Volta, Central and Eastern, and runs against them in Brong Ahafo, Ashanti and Western; and the MTE gap is negative in every region except Eastern, where it is not significant, and largest in Upper East. The crop and regional patterns do not sort neatly by agro-ecology or by cash-crop status, since the smallest and among the largest technology gaps are both in southern regions, and they do not line up with the density of financial services in Table 2, so we do not attempt to attribute them. What they establish is that the technology gap is pervasive rather than concentrated in a few systems, while the efficiency contrast varies in sign from one setting to another, which is more consistent with readings that operate through the household, such as loan use and selection, than with one that operates through the lending environment.

For targeting, the heterogeneity results cut two ways. Because the technology gap is negative in nearly every subgroup, there is no identifiable class of borrowers, defined by service use, gender, age, schooling, crop or region, for whom credit use is associated with a technology closer to best practice; cocoa producers and, on the efficiency margin, cooperative and credit-union members are the nearest to exceptions. Where the subgroups differ is in whether credit users make up part of the technology gap through better within-technology performance, as unbanked households, younger and female operators and plantain and groundnut producers do, or compound it, as banked households, the most educated operators and susu participants do. That is a statement about where managerial support would and would not find a deficit to close, and about the fact that the subgroups in which the overall shortfall is largest, account holders and the post-secondary educated, are not those a financial-inclusion programme would ordinarily prioritize; it is not evidence that credit itself works better for some groups than for others.

6. Conclusion

This paper asked whether the credit that Ghanaian crop-farming households obtain is associated with operating a better production technology, with using a given technology more efficiently, or with neither, and whether the answer depends on who in the household borrows, on the other financial services the household uses, and on the operator, the crop and the region. The question matters because the two margins call for different policy responses, and because the case for extending finance to smallholders rests on the first of them: credit is expected to relax the liquidity constraint that keeps farms from adopting best-practice technology. We addressed it with the farmer-level records of the two most recent rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, a household-level indicator of credit use rebuilt from the original questionnaires, group-specific stochastic frontiers enveloped by a stochastic metafrontier and estimated on a sample in which each credit-using household is paired with an observably similar non-user, and inference from a jackknife that re-runs matching and estimation in every replicate. Credit use is rare in this population, at 8.9% of operators, and the descriptive record of Section 3 showed that the loans behind that figure are mostly informal or group-based, mostly unsecured, mostly not for farming where their purpose can be observed, and obtained in an environment in which the modal non-borrower reports no need for a loan.

The answers to the three questions are consistent with one another and run against the hypothesis that motivated the analysis. First, credit-using and non-using households do operate different technologies, but the difference is not the one a liquidity-constraint story predicts: the group frontiers differ mainly in a higher responsiveness of output to family labour among credit users, with identical returns to land and negligible differences for purchased inputs, and matched credit users apply less fertilizer, planting material, hired labour and pesticide per hectare than their comparators while producing about as much. Second, the performance shortfall of credit users relative to best practice is a technology gap, not an efficiency gap. In the matched sample the technology gap ratio of credit-using households is 0.877 against 0.929 for their matched non-users, a shortfall of 5.3 percentage points: the technology set operated by borrowing households lies farther inside the best-practice frontier, not nearer to it. Technical efficiency within each group’s own technology differs by an amount that is small and not stable in sign, and meta-frontier efficiency is correspondingly lower for credit users, by between 2.9 and 4.3 percentage points depending on the specification. Balancing the two groups on observables removed almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and little of the technology gap, which locates the credit-associated shortfall in the frontier borrowing households operate rather than in how they manage it. Third, the technology gap is pervasive. It holds under every definition of which household member borrowed, every matching scheme, functional form, efficiency estimator and aggregation rule, and within every financial-service subgroup, every gender, age and education group, every region, and every major crop except cocoa, where credit users sit slightly closer to the frontier, and sorghum, where the two groups do not differ. The efficiency contrast, by contrast, varies in sign from one setting to another, and the overall shortfall is concentrated among households that also hold a formal account and among the most educated operators, the groups in which a complementarity between credit and other financial services would have been expected to show.

These are findings; what follows is interpretation, and the design bounds it. The estimates are associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample. Four readings of the negative technology gap are consistent with the evidence. The one the exhibits most directly support is that household credit in this population mostly does not finance the farm: fewer than one in three loans were taken for agricultural purposes in the round in which purpose can be observed, credit is fungible within the household, and borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs, so the indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. The others are selection into borrowing on characteristics the survey does not record, the pooling of unconstrained non-borrowers with constrained ones in the comparison group, and the attenuation that misreported informal loans would produce, which cannot explain the sign. The data cannot rank these readings, and none of them implies that extending credit would lower the technology a given farm operates. What the results rule out is the account in which household credit, as farm households in Ghana actually obtained it between 2012/13 and 2016/17, is associated with movement toward the best-practice technology. They do not show that agricultural credit fails to raise farm technology, because the credit observed here is for the most part not agricultural credit; the distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper’s substantive contribution to a Ghanaian literature that has so far studied credit tied to particular crops, schemes and regions against a single frontier.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions, and they are specific rather than generic. The estimation sample is a complete-case sample formed at two stacked points: the harmonized financial module retains operators aged eighteen or more with recorded age, schooling, account and insurance status, and the financial-inclusion index that enters the matching distance is built on complete cases of the same indicators; the matching then requires complete information on every matching covariate. Neither restriction is guaranteed to be random with respect to financial-service use, so the matched contrast describes the completely observed population of credit users and their nearest comparators rather than the population of Ghanaian crop farmers. The index itself is a summary rather than a measurement, and Note S1 now sets out what it does and does not capture: it is the first principal component of fourteen indicators of schooling, financial-sector employment, insurance holding and account ownership, fitted within survey-round and locality strata and min-max scaled over the pooled sample, and the component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in that indicator set, roughly twice the fourteenth an uninformative component would take, so it is informative but far from dominant. Its content is also not identical across the two rounds: travel insurance has too little variation to enter the component in either 2016/17 stratum, so thirteen indicators rather than fourteen underlie the index there, and the account-ownership item recognizes mobile-money accounts only in that round. A different indicator set or scaling would therefore change which non-user is paired with which user, and although the estimates are stable across eight matching schemes, their sensitivity to the index specification has not been examined directly, and nothing here should be read as an effect of inclusion as an index. The indicator records credit use rather than access, so the contrast is between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained. Matching cannot balance managerial ability, risk preference, land quality, wealth outside the surveyed modules or standing with the group-based lenders that supplied a rising share of loans, the survey offers no credible instrument, and the design assumes that lending to one household does not change the terms available to its neighbours, an assumption that group lending intermediated through the same communities makes uncomfortable. Finally, the data are repeated cross-sections in which credit use and production are observed in the same survey interview, so the estimates cannot separate credit that finances this season’s technology from credit that follows a bad one, and they say nothing about the trajectory of a farm’s technology after a loan.

Within these limits the implications for policy are clear about direction if not about mechanism. Expanding the volume of household credit as such should not be expected to close the technology gap in Ghanaian crop production, because the households that borrow are not, on this evidence, the ones operating the best-practice technology, and their loans are not observable as an intensification of the farm. The shortfall is not managerial, so extension and training aimed at how borrowers use their inputs would not find the deficit they were designed to close. The evidence instead points to the conditions under which credit becomes farm investment: loan products sized and timed for crop production, bundled with the input supply, advisory services and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking, in a setting where distance and collateral requirements have already fallen while the share of farmers reporting no need for a loan rose from 55.4% to 63.7%. The variables the estimates associate with proximity to the best-practice technology, extension contact, mechanization and secure tenure, are those a technology-oriented policy would act on, and cocoa, the one crop with sector-specific input and extension arrangements, is the one crop in which credit users are not at a technological disadvantage. Whether these associations reflect what such arrangements do, or who selects into them, is exactly what the present design cannot say.

Three lines of research would resolve what this study cannot. Panel data on the same households, or a source of variation in credit access unrelated to farm performance of the kind that experimental relaxations of credit and risk constraints have supplied for Ghanaian farm households [19], would separate the technology in use before borrowing from the technology after it and would distinguish credit that finances investment from credit that follows a shock. Survey modules that link the purpose and source of each loan to the plot on which inputs are applied, and that elicit credit-constraint status directly rather than borrowing alone, would allow the loan-use and use-versus-access readings to be tested rather than argued from aggregate purpose shares. And a decomposition of the credit contrast by loan source, which the estimation objects already carry but no exhibit reports, would show whether the technology gap is a feature of relational and group-based borrowing in particular or of household borrowing in general. Until such evidence exists, the appropriate reading of these results is that financial inclusion in Ghana has broadened on the savings and payments margin faster than on the credit margin, that the credit farm households do obtain is not associated with better production technology, and that the policy problem is less the supply of loans than the design of products that farm households would borrow for and invest on the farm. For a financial-inclusion agenda that expects credit to carry farms toward the frontier, the question this raises is not how to lend more but what the loans that farm households already take are buying.

Appendix

Note S1. Financial-Inclusion Index Construction

The financial-inclusion index introduced in Section 2.3 and used as a matching covariate in Section 4.3 summarizes the non-credit dimensions of a farm household member’s engagement with financial services. It is built on one record per household member, with that member’s demographic characteristics averaged over the plots the member works, merged by enumeration area, household and member identifier to the harmonized financial-services release from which the indicators of Table S0 are drawn. The index is the first principal component of 14 indicators: the member’s years of schooling, whether the member works in a financial institution, whether another member of the household does, whether the member owns an account with a financial institution or contributes to a savings scheme, and ten indicators of insurance cover (vehicle, medical, funeral, property, commercial, travel, life, retirement, education and other endowment or investment plans). The component is fitted on complete cases across all 14 indicators; on the current release the financial indicators are themselves complete, so that restriction binds only through years of schooling, which is carried down from the farmer file. Composite measures of this kind are standard in work that treats financial inclusion as a multidimensional construct spanning accounts, savings and insurance rather than as account ownership alone, in Africa as elsewhere [1], [3].

Three indicators available in the same release were deliberately left out: the community distances to the nearest bank, motorable road and public transport (Table S0). Coverage is the first reason. The community questionnaire is administered per enumeration area and does not reach every area, so the three distances are missing for about a fifth of the members in the release, and the complete-case rule would drop every one of them. That loss is not random. It falls disproportionately on urban enumeration areas in 2012/13, which is precisely the imbalance the harmonization avoids by joining the community block to the farmer records rather than restricting to it, so admitting the distances here would reintroduce the same selection one stage later. Construct is the second reason. The distances describe a place rather than a person and enter with the sign opposite to every other indicator, so a component that included them would mix how financially connected a member is with how far that member lives from a bank. Excluding them makes the index unambiguously the former and removes the need to reason about sign when the loadings are read.

Because the two rounds differ in the services they record and rural and urban localities differ in the services available, a component is fitted separately within each survey-round-by-locality stratum rather than once over the pooled data: on 8,083 members in rural GLSS6, 1,527 in urban GLSS6, 5,692 in rural GLSS7 and 971 in urban GLSS7, against 16,273 in the pooled fit that supplies the reference metric. The sign and the scale of a principal component are arbitrary, so the four stratum scores are not comparable as estimated. Each is therefore placed on the pooled component’s metric by regressing the pooled score on the stratum score within the stratum and retaining the fitted values, a rescaling that fixes orientation as well as scale: where a stratum’s component came out sign-flipped, the regression coefficient is negative and the fitted values still align with the pooled score. The strata are disjoint, so the rescaled scores coalesce into a single value for every member. Three variables are released. FinIdx is the rescaled component itself. FinIdxSi is FinIdx min-max scaled over the pooled sample to the unit interval, and it is the variable that enters the matching distance of Section 4.3. FinIdxCat is the weighted quintiles of FinIdx, also taken over the pooled sample. Both transformations are pooled rather than within-round, so they express a member’s absolute position on the index and not a rank within a survey round; and because the scaling is min-max, FinIdxSi is by construction sensitive to a single extreme value, which compresses the remaining members into a narrower band than a rank or quantile transform would.

Table S6 reports the first-component loadings and the share of variance the component explains in each stratum, and they warrant a careful reading rather than a reassuring one. In the pooled fit every loading is positive and the two largest are on years of schooling and on account ownership, followed by life and vehicle insurance and by financial-sector employment, so the pooled metric is oriented in the direction the index’s name implies and the rescaling carries that orientation into every stratum. Two departures qualify this. Travel insurance has no variation in either 2016/17 stratum and is screened out of both, so the index rests on 14 indicators in 2012/13 and on 13 in 2016/17; taken with the fact that account ownership captures mobile money only in the later round, the index’s content is not identical across the two rounds. And one loading is negative: commercial insurance in the urban 2016/17 stratum. It is near enough to zero to carry little weight in the score, but a mixed sign pattern is the signal that a first component is picking up something other than inclusion, and it is reported here rather than smoothed over. The more consequential diagnostic is the explained variance. The first component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in a set of 14 indicators, where a component carrying no information at all would account for about a fourteenth. The component is therefore informative but far from dominant: the indicators it summarizes are only loosely correlated with one another, a single dimension does not come close to exhausting them, and a different indicator set or a different scaling would produce a different ordering of members. This is the substantiation of the limitation that Section 6 states, and it is the reason the index is used to balance a comparison rather than to carry an interpretation.

What the index is not, finally, is the treatment. The treatment throughout this paper is credit_hh, the household credit indicator defined in Section 2.2 and documented in Table S0. The index enters in two other roles: FinIdxSi is one covariate in the distance on which each credit-using household is paired with a non-user, so that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services (Section 4.3), and FinIdxCat is available in the estimation as a dimension of heterogeneity. No exhibit in this paper reports results by the index’s quintiles; heterogeneity across financial services is examined on the observed indicators themselves, formal account ownership above all (Figure 2 and Table 6). The index is estimated on 16,273 household-member records, a larger set than the 15,860 farm operators of the analysis sample, so index values exist for records the frontier analysis does not use; the matching draws on the values it needs and discards the rest.

Notes: Items are drawn from Part B, Section 12a of each questionnaire (sec12a in GLSS6, g7sec12a in GLSS7); GLSS7 suffixes multi-response items with _a, _b and so on, which the harmonization strips. Wording is reproduced from the survey instruments. Loan detail is elicited only from respondents who applied and were granted a loan, so the credit indicator is the conjunction of application, approval and a positive amount rather than a test on the amount alone. Mobile money and susu accounts do not appear in the GLSS6 instrument, so their zero entries in Table 2 denote items not asked rather than an absence of holdings; the GLSS6 columns for the remaining institution and account items are re-indexed onto the GLSS7 positions before the rounds are pooled. GLSS7 records the status, source, purpose and collateral of up to three loans but a single loan amount, and adds a “processing” outcome that GLSS6 does not offer. The source-of-knowledge item is reported in Table 2 but is not discussed in the text; its derived category indicators do not currently reproduce the response order shown above, and the block is withheld from the narrative pending correction. Distances are taken from the community questionnaire rather than from Section 12a.

The table states the specification rather than any estimate. Frontier, shifter and inefficiency rows are the arguments passed in 004_MSF_financial_inclusion_study.R; matching rows are the covariate lists of 002_MATCHING_financial_inclusion_study.R. The corresponding estimates are in Tables 4, S3 and S4.

Expected signs are the a priori expectations of Section 4.1, not findings. An em dash marks a variable for which the paper posits no expectation; "Not applicable" marks a variable that enters an exact-match stratum or a matching distance rather than a regression, so that no coefficient sign exists to expect. The criterion for the matching covariates is balance between users and non-users, reported for each of them in Fig. S1.

The inefficiency covariates scale the variance of the one-sided error term, so a positive coefficient means greater inefficiency and, in Equation (3), a larger technology gap; a negative expected sign therefore means the variable is expected to place the farm closer to its frontier. 004_MSF passes the same vector as inefficiency_covariates and as adoption_covariates, so each row in that block governs both margins.

Positive signs on the six inputs follow from monotonicity of the production function and are not a prediction about credit. H3 of Section 4.1 is a prediction about a difference of elasticities between groups -- credit users' frontier more responsive to land and labour, and not more responsive to fertilizer -- which no single row can carry.

004_MSF passes the survey round as a factor in both the frontier shifters and the inefficiency determinants, but Tables S3 and S4 print no round coefficient; see the note to those tables.

The treatment, credit_hh, is not listed because it is a regressor in none of the three specifications: it partitions the sample into the groups whose frontiers are compared (Section 4.2) and supplies the flag on which pairs are drawn (Section 4.3). It is documented in Table S0. Pairing further requires complete information on the identifiers, the survey weight and the treatment flag, and an observation missing any matching field is dropped before pairs are formed.

Data source: Ghana Living Standards Survey [waves 6-7].

Entries are loadings on the first principal component, estimated over the pooled sample and separately within each survey-round-by-locality stratum by 000_INDEX_financial_inclusion_study.do. GLSS6 is the 2012/13 round and GLSS7 the 2016/17 round.

Rows are ordered by the pooled loading, largest first. An em dash marks an indicator that does not enter a stratum's component: it has no variation in that stratum and is screened out before estimation, so the loading is absent rather than zero, as with travel insurance. The component rests on 14 indicators in 2012/13 and 13 in 2016/17, so its content is not identical across the two rounds.

Loadings are as estimated within each stratum, before the stratum scores are placed on the pooled component's metric. The sign and scale of a principal component are arbitrary, so a sign pattern is informative within a column and not across columns; in the pooled fit every loading is positive, so a higher index score means greater financial inclusion, and the rescaling carries that orientation into every stratum (Note S1).

The share of variance explained is the proportion of the total variance of the indicator set carried by the first component. With 14 indicators, a component carrying no more than an equal share would account for about 0.071.

Observations are household-member records. The index is estimated on more records than the analysis sample of farm operators uses; the matching draws the values it needs (Note S1).
